questions.title: The Option Greeks and Delta-Hedging
questions.prompt: Define delta, gamma, vega, and theta for a long call option, and explain why a market maker's delta-hedge needs to be rebalanced rather than set once.
questions.code:
Call delta = N(d1) in [0,1]
Gamma = dDelta/dS, always positive for long options
Vega = dV/d(sigma), positive for long options
Theta = dV/dt, typically negative for long options
questions.modelAnswer: Delta (∂V/∂S) measures how much the option's value changes per $1 move in the underlying; for a call it's N(d1), ranging from 0 to 1. Gamma (∂Delta/∂S) measures how fast delta itself changes as the underlying moves, and is always positive for a long option. Vega (∂V/∂σ) measures sensitivity to volatility and is positive for long calls and puts alike, since more volatility raises the value of the right to choose only favorable outcomes. Theta (∂V/∂t) measures sensitivity to time passing and is typically negative for a long option — every day that passes without a favorable move erodes time value. A dealer who sells a call is short delta and buys delta shares of stock to neutralize that exposure, but delta is only accurate for a small, instantaneous move — because gamma is nonzero, delta itself shifts as the stock moves, so a hedge that was neutral a moment ago drifts out of balance and has to be recalculated and rebalanced, with high-gamma positions needing far more frequent rebalancing than low-gamma ones.
questions.professionalAnswer: I think of delta as the snapshot and gamma as the warning label on that snapshot — delta tells you the hedge ratio right now, gamma tells you how quickly that hedge ratio is about to be wrong. A desk with a lot of short-dated, at-the-money options is going to be rebalancing constantly because gamma peaks exactly there; a desk holding deep in- or out-of-the-money options barely needs to touch their hedge because gamma is close to zero. Vega and theta I'd describe as the other two axes of risk a book is carrying even when delta is perfectly flat — you can be delta-neutral and still have a very real view (intentional or not) on volatility and time decay.
questions.example: A dealer short one call with delta 0.60 buys 60 shares per contract (100-share multiplier) to hedge. If the stock rallies and delta rises to 0.75 because of positive gamma, the hedge is now under-sized by 15 shares per contract and must be topped up to stay neutral.
commonMistakes: Treating delta as a fixed, static number rather than something that changes with the stock price
Forgetting that gamma is the reason a delta-hedge needs rebalancing, not just general market noise
Mixing up the sign of theta (often negative for long options) with vega (positive for long options)
Assuming gamma differs between an equivalent call and put — it's identical at the same strike and expiration
keyPoints: Delta = N(d1) for a call; measures sensitivity to the underlying
Gamma = rate of change of delta; always positive for long options, peaks near at-the-money, short-dated
Vega measures volatility sensitivity; positive for long options
Theta measures time decay; typically negative for long options
Gamma is precisely why a delta-hedge must be dynamically rebalanced

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines all four Greeks with correct signs
Correctly explains delta-hedging mechanics
Explains gamma's role in requiring rebalancing
Uses a clear, concrete example

questions.title: CAPM, Beta, and the Security Market Line
questions.prompt: State the CAPM formula and explain why it uses beta rather than total standard deviation as the risk measure that determines expected return. What's the difference between the Security Market Line and the Capital Market Line?
questions.code:
E[Ri] = Rf + beta_i * (E[Rm] - Rf)
beta_i = Cov(Ri, Rm) / Var(Rm)
questions.modelAnswer: CAPM states that an asset's expected return equals the risk-free rate plus beta times the market risk premium. Beta, not total standard deviation, is the relevant risk measure because in a world where everyone holds a well-diversified portfolio, unsystematic (asset-specific) risk has already been diversified away and the market doesn't compensate anyone for voluntarily holding it; only systematic risk — the risk that doesn't diversify away — earns a return premium, and beta is precisely the measure of how much systematic risk an asset carries relative to the market. Total σ mixes systematic and unsystematic risk together, so using it would reward investors for bearing risk they could have diversified away for free. The Security Market Line plots expected return against beta and is the direct graph of the CAPM formula itself — every correctly priced asset, diversified or not, sits exactly on it. The Capital Market Line plots expected return against total risk (σ) for portfolios combining the risk-free asset and the market portfolio, and only efficient portfolios sit on it — individual, non-diversified assets generally plot below it.
questions.professionalAnswer: The beta-versus-sigma distinction is the one thing I'd make sure comes across clearly, because it's the most commonly garbled part of CAPM in interviews — people say 'risk' and mean total volatility, but CAPM is specifically pricing only the piece of volatility you can't diversify away. SML and CML trip people up constantly too: SML is beta on the x-axis and it's a statement about every individual asset; CML is total risk on the x-axis and only describes portfolios that are actual combinations of the market and cash. If someone asks me to draw one versus the other, that's the distinction I lead with.
questions.example: Rf=3%, Rm=9%, beta=1.4. E[Ri] = 0.03 + 1.4*(0.09-0.03) = 0.03 + 0.084 = 11.4%. The stock's position on the SML is pinned exactly by its beta of 1.4, regardless of whether it's part of a diversified portfolio.
commonMistakes: Using total standard deviation instead of beta in the CAPM formula
Confusing the SML (beta vs. return, all assets) with the CML (total risk vs. return, efficient portfolios only)
Forgetting that beta is Cov(Ri,Rm)/Var(Rm), not just correlation
Assuming a high-beta asset is automatically a 'riskier' investment in every sense, ignoring that beta only captures systematic risk
keyPoints: CAPM: E[Ri] = Rf + beta(E[Rm]-Rf)
Beta isolates systematic risk, which is the only risk that earns a premium under CAPM
SML: expected return vs. beta, true for every correctly priced asset
CML: expected return vs. total risk, true only for efficient portfolios combining the market and the risk-free asset

evaluationCriteria.criterion: States the CAPM formula and beta formula correctly
Explains why systematic risk alone is priced
Correctly distinguishes SML from CML
Provides a correct worked example

questions.title: Implied Volatility and the Volatility Skew
questions.prompt: What is implied volatility, why does finding it require numerical root-finding rather than a closed-form solution, and what does the volatility skew in equity index options tell us about real-world return distributions?
questions.modelAnswer: Implied volatility is the σ that, plugged into Black-Scholes along with the observable inputs (S, K, r, T), reproduces the option's actual market price. Because σ sits inside the N(d1) and N(d2) cumulative normal terms in a way that can't be algebraically isolated, there's no closed-form way to solve for it directly — practitioners use iterative root-finding methods like Newton-Raphson or bisection, guessing a σ, computing the resulting price, and adjusting until it matches the market price closely enough. If Black-Scholes's constant-volatility assumption actually held, every option on the same underlying and expiration would produce the same implied volatility regardless of strike. In practice, equity index options show a skew — IV is higher for low strikes (downside puts) and lower for high strikes — reflecting demand for crash protection and the fact that real returns have fatter tails and show volatility clustering, not the lognormal, constant-volatility process Black-Scholes assumes.
questions.professionalAnswer: The key thing I try to convey is that implied volatility isn't really a volatility forecast in the purest sense — it's the market's own correction for everything Black-Scholes gets wrong, encoded into one number per strike and expiration. The skew specifically is the market saying 'I think a crash is more likely, or at least more painful, than a lognormal model would predict,' and that's exactly why desks price every option off its own point on the surface rather than one flat number. If someone asks me to explain the skew without reaching for jargon, I'd just say: people pay up for downside insurance, and that shows up as higher implied vol on the low strikes.
questions.example: A one-month at-the-money call implying 16% volatility next to a one-month 10%-out-of-the-money put implying 22% volatility is the skew in action — the market prices more expected downside movement into that put than a single constant-σ Black-Scholes model would predict.
commonMistakes: Thinking implied volatility can be solved for algebraically like the other Black-Scholes inputs
Confusing the volatility skew (varies by strike) with the term structure (varies by expiration)
Treating implied volatility as a pure forecast rather than a market-implied correction for model misspecification
Assuming the smile/skew is a mispricing to be arbitraged away rather than real evidence about return distributions
keyPoints: Implied volatility is Black-Scholes solved backward from an observed market price
Requires numerical root-finding since sigma can't be isolated algebraically
Volatility skew: IV varies by strike at a fixed expiration
The skew is evidence of fat tails and demand for downside protection, not a flaw in the market

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines implied volatility
Explains why root-finding is required
Correctly describes the equity skew and its direction
Connects the skew to fat tails / crash-protection demand

questions.title: Computing Call and Put Delta
questions.prompt: Using Black-Scholes with S=$80, K=$75, r=4%, σ=25%, T=0.5 years: compute d1, then the call and put deltas, and state how many shares a dealer who sold (wrote) 10 call contracts (100 shares/contract) should buy to delta-hedge the position.
questions.code:
d1 = [ln(S/K) + (r + sigma^2/2)*T] / (sigma*sqrt(T))
Call delta = N(d1)
Put delta = N(d1) - 1
questions.modelAnswer: d1 = [ln(80/75) + (0.04 + 0.25^2/2)*0.5] / (0.25*sqrt(0.5)) = [0.0645 + 0.035625] / 0.17678 ≈ 0.100125 / 0.17678 ≈ 0.566. N(0.566) ≈ 0.714, so the call delta is about 0.71 and the put delta is about 0.71 - 1 = -0.29. The dealer wrote (is short) 10 call contracts, i.e. 1,000 shares' worth of delta exposure at 0.71 delta each, giving a short-delta exposure of roughly -714 shares. To delta-hedge, the dealer should buy approximately 714 shares of the underlying, bringing the combined position's delta close to zero for small moves in the stock.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through this exactly the way I'd do it on a desk: compute d1 first, convert it to N(d1) for the call delta, subtract 1 for the put delta, then multiply by the position size and the 100-share multiplier to get total shares. Being short calls means being short delta, so the hedge is a stock purchase, not a sale — that sign is the part people most often get backwards under time pressure, and it's worth double-checking out loud before giving a final number.
questions.example: d1 ≈ 0.566, N(d1) ≈ 0.714 → call delta ≈ 0.714, put delta ≈ -0.286. Short 10 contracts (1,000 shares notional) × 0.714 ≈ 714 shares of short-delta exposure → buy ≈714 shares to hedge.
commonMistakes: Getting the sign of the hedge backwards (selling instead of buying shares when short calls)
Forgetting the 100-share-per-contract multiplier when scaling delta to an actual share count
Computing put delta as N(-d1) instead of N(d1)-1 (both are mathematically equivalent, but mixing conventions causes sign errors)
Dropping the σ²/2 term inside d1's numerator
keyPoints: d1 combines moneyness, rate, volatility, and time into one normalized term
Call delta = N(d1); put delta = N(d1) - 1
Being short calls means being short delta; the hedge is to buy shares
Must scale per-share delta by contract multiplier and number of contracts

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes d1
Correctly derives call and put delta from d1
Correctly scales to total shares and multiplier
Gets the hedge direction (buy, not sell) right

questions.title: Modified Duration and Price Sensitivity
questions.prompt: A bond has a Macaulay duration of 4.2 years and a yield to maturity of 6%. Compute its modified duration, then estimate the percentage price change if yields rise by 75 basis points.
questions.code:
Modified Duration = Macaulay Duration / (1+y)
Percent price change ≈ -ModDur * Δy
questions.modelAnswer: Modified duration = 4.2 / 1.06 ≈ 3.962. For a 75bp (0.75 percentage point) rise in yields, the estimated price change is approximately -3.962 × 0.0075 ≈ -0.0297, i.e. the bond's price is expected to fall by roughly 2.97%. This is a linear (first-order) approximation; for a larger yield move the estimate would need a convexity correction term to stay accurate.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd just plug straight into the formula — Macaulay duration divided by one plus the yield gives modified duration, then negative modified duration times the yield change gives the approximate percentage price move. For 75 basis points that's a small enough move that the linear approximation is reasonably trustworthy; I'd flag that for anything much bigger than this I'd want to add the convexity term to avoid understating the price change.
commonMistakes: Using Macaulay duration directly instead of converting to modified duration
Forgetting the negative sign (yields up, price down)
Expressing the yield change as 0.75 instead of 0.0075
Treating the linear duration estimate as exact rather than an approximation that ignores convexity
keyPoints: Modified duration = Macaulay duration / (1+y)
Percentage price change ≈ -modified duration × yield change
The approximation is linear and ignores convexity, which matters more for larger yield moves

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes modified duration
Correctly computes the estimated price change
Notes the approximation is linear / ignores convexity

questions.title: Sharpe vs. Sortino for an Asymmetric Strategy
questions.prompt: A strategy has a daily mean return of 0.04%, daily total volatility of 0.9%, and daily downside deviation (below 0%) of 0.5%. The risk-free rate is 0. Annualize both the Sharpe and Sortino ratios (using √252) and explain what the gap between them tells you about the strategy's return shape.
questions.code:
Sharpe_ann = (mean/sigma_total) * sqrt(252)
Sortino_ann = (mean/sigma_downside) * sqrt(252)
questions.modelAnswer: Daily Sharpe = 0.0004/0.009 ≈ 0.0444; annualized ×√252 (≈15.87) ≈ 0.70. Daily Sortino = 0.0004/0.005 = 0.08; annualized ≈ 1.27. The Sortino ratio is noticeably higher than the Sharpe ratio, which happens because downside deviation (0.5%) is much smaller than total volatility (0.9%) — meaning most of this strategy's volatility is coming from upside moves, not downside ones. That pattern is consistent with a strategy that has small, frequent losses and occasional larger gains (e.g., a trend-following-style payoff), since the Sharpe ratio penalizes that upside volatility just as harshly as downside volatility, while the Sortino ratio only penalizes the downside.
questions.professionalAnswer: Whenever I see Sortino meaningfully above Sharpe, my first instinct is: this return stream is probably positively skewed, with its volatility concentrated on the upside. That's a good sign, not a red flag, because it means the 'risk' the Sharpe ratio is punishing is partly just the strategy occasionally making a lot of money. I'd want to see the actual return histogram to confirm, but the gap alone is already informative before I look at a single chart.
questions.example: Sharpe_ann ≈ 0.0444 × 15.87 ≈ 0.70. Sortino_ann ≈ 0.08 × 15.87 ≈ 1.27. The roughly 0.57 gap between them points to upside-skewed volatility.
commonMistakes: Annualizing only one of the two ratios and comparing a daily number to an annualized one
Assuming Sharpe and Sortino should always be close together
Interpreting a higher Sortino than Sharpe as a red flag rather than a sign of favorable return asymmetry
Using total volatility in the Sortino ratio instead of downside-only deviation
keyPoints: Sharpe divides excess return by total volatility; Sortino divides it by downside-only deviation
Both are annualized the same way, by multiplying the daily ratio by √252
A much higher Sortino than Sharpe suggests upside-skewed (favorable) return asymmetry
A much lower Sortino than Sharpe would suggest the opposite — small steady gains and rare large losses

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes annualized Sharpe
Correctly computes annualized Sortino
Correctly interprets the gap as upside-skewed volatility
Notes what the opposite gap direction would imply

questions.title: Backtest Sharpe of 2.5, Live Sharpe Near Zero
questions.prompt: A high-frequency mean-reversion strategy backtested with a Sharpe of 2.5 is now live and tracking close to a Sharpe of 0, even though the signal's direction still looks correct day to day. Walk through how you'd diagnose this, and name the single most likely culprit for a high-turnover strategy like this one.
questions.modelAnswer: The first thing to check for a high-turnover strategy is whether the backtest honestly modeled transaction costs and slippage, since costs scale with how often a strategy trades, not with how much capital it manages — a strategy rebalancing daily pays its round-trip cost roughly 252 times a year, which can easily consume all the apparent edge even at a modest cost-per-trade. I'd re-run the backtest with a realistic cost model (a per-trade cost in basis points on every position change, plus volatility-scaled slippage that works against the trader) and see how much of the 2.5 Sharpe survives. I'd also check for look-ahead bias in the original backtest and confirm the signal wasn't selected via extensive in-sample parameter search, since both would separately inflate the backtested number, but given the signal direction still looks correct live, the cost/turnover explanation is the most likely single culprit here.
questions.professionalAnswer: With a high-frequency, high-turnover strategy, costs are always my first suspect before I even look at anything more exotic — a backtest that charged zero or near-zero cost per trade can show a fantastic Sharpe that simply isn't achievable once you pay the spread and slippage on every single rebalance. I'd re-cost the backtest honestly and see how much of that 2.5 survives; if it collapses toward zero under realistic costs, that's the answer, and if it doesn't, then I'd start looking at look-ahead bias or overfitting next.
commonMistakes: Jumping straight to 'the market regime changed' without first checking cost realism
Assuming a correct-looking signal direction rules out an execution-cost explanation
Modeling transaction costs as a flat, volatility-independent number instead of scaling with turnover and market conditions
Not separating slippage (market-driven) from market impact (self-caused) when diagnosing the gap
keyPoints: Transaction costs scale with trading frequency (turnover), not capital
A high-turnover strategy backtested with unrealistic or zero costs will show an inflated Sharpe
Re-costing the backtest honestly is the direct diagnostic step
Look-ahead bias and overfitting are separate possible culprits worth ruling out too

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Identifies transaction costs/slippage as the most likely culprit for a high-turnover strategy
Explains why turnover amplifies cost drag
Proposes a concrete diagnostic step (re-cost the backtest)
Mentions other plausible secondary causes to rule out

questions.title: A 'Market-Neutral' Book That Wasn't, During a Crash
questions.prompt: A long/short equity book normally shows a beta to the S&P 500 near 0.05, yet it lost sharply during a sudden market-wide selloff. The PM is confused since the book is supposed to be market-neutral. What's the likely explanation, and how would you explain it?
questions.modelAnswer: This is the correlation-to-one effect: a dollar-neutral book's low average beta comes from the long leg and short leg moving mostly independently under normal conditions, so their exposures roughly cancel. In a sudden, broad market panic, every sector and name tends to sell off together instead of independently — the correlation structure the hedge depended on collapses toward 1 across almost everything, and the book's realized beta during the event can spike well above its normal near-zero level, even though the position sizes and construction never changed. I'd explain to the PM that dollar-neutral construction reduces net market exposure on average, not always, and that a broad macro shock is precisely the scenario where long/short diversification is weakest, since that's exactly when every position starts moving in the same direction at once.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the PM directly: being dollar-neutral by construction doesn't mean market-neutral in every environment, and a panic is the one environment where that gap shows up hardest, because correlations across names and sectors move toward one right when you need them to stay low. I'd want to show the actual realized beta during the event versus its typical level, since that single number usually makes the mechanism click immediately, and I'd use it to start a conversation about whether the book needs an explicit macro/tail hedge on top of its usual construction.
commonMistakes: Assuming dollar-neutral and market-neutral mean the same thing in every market environment
Treating the loss as evidence the hedge was built incorrectly rather than a known, real correlation effect
Not quantifying the realized beta spike to make the explanation concrete
Failing to propose any forward-looking response (e.g., an explicit tail hedge) after explaining the cause
keyPoints: Dollar-neutral construction reduces average market exposure, not exposure in every regime
Correlation-to-one: cross-sectional diversification breaks down when everything sells off together
Realized beta can spike well above its typical level during a panic even with no change in positioning
Worth proposing an explicit macro or tail hedge as a forward-looking response

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the correlation-to-one mechanism
Distinguishes dollar-neutral from market-neutral clearly
Communicates this in PM-appropriate, non-defensive language
Suggests a forward-looking risk-management response

questions.title: Structuring VaR Reporting Across Multiple Desks
questions.prompt: You're asked to design how VaR gets reported across five trading desks that roll up into one firm-wide risk report. What considerations go into aggregating desk-level VaR into a firm-wide number, and why can't you just sum the desks' individual VaRs?
questions.modelAnswer: Each desk's VaR should be computed consistently — same confidence level, same horizon, and ideally the same methodology (parametric, historical, or Monte Carlo) — so the numbers are comparable before any aggregation happens. Simply summing the five desks' VaRs overstates firm-wide risk, because VaR is not generally sub-additive and desk-level losses are not perfectly correlated: on most days, some desks will be up while others are down, so the firm's combined loss distribution is narrower than the naive sum of each desk's worst-case threshold would suggest. A proper aggregation needs either a firm-wide correlation/covariance matrix across desks' P&L (to compute a true portfolio-level VaR) or a consistent historical-simulation/Monte Carlo approach run at the firm level using each desk's actual position data, not just its standalone VaR number. The report should show both the firm-wide aggregated VaR and each desk's standalone VaR side by side, since the gap between the sum of standalones and the true aggregate is itself informative about how much diversification benefit exists across desks.
questions.professionalAnswer: The thing I'd push back on immediately if someone just wanted to add five VaR numbers together is that it throws away the one benefit that makes a multi-desk firm safer than five independent funds — the fact that desks don't all lose money on the same day. I'd want the firm-wide number built from actual position-level correlations across desks, not from summing already-computed standalone numbers, and I'd report the standalone sum alongside the true aggregate specifically so people can see how much of a diversification benefit the firm is actually getting.
commonMistakes: Simply summing standalone desk VaRs as the firm-wide number
Using inconsistent confidence levels or horizons across desks before aggregating
Ignoring cross-desk correlation entirely when it's the whole point of aggregation
Reporting only the aggregate number without showing the standalone comparison that reveals diversification benefit
keyPoints: Desk-level VaR must be computed on a consistent basis (confidence, horizon, method) before aggregating
VaR is not sub-additive; summing standalone VaRs overstates true combined risk
True aggregation requires cross-desk correlation or position-level simulation
Reporting both the standalone sum and the true aggregate reveals the firm's actual diversification benefit

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains why simple summation overstates risk
Proposes a correlation-aware or position-level aggregation approach
Notes the need for consistent methodology across desks
Recommends reporting both standalone and aggregate figures

questions.title: The Practical Limits of Mean-Variance Optimization
questions.prompt: Walk through what mean-variance optimization actually needs as inputs, and explain why, for a portfolio of several hundred stocks, naively estimating the full covariance matrix from historical returns is a real practical problem, not just a theoretical one.
questions.modelAnswer: Mean-variance optimization needs a vector of expected returns (μ) for every asset and a full covariance matrix (Σ) capturing every asset's variance and every pairwise covariance. For N assets, Σ has N(N+1)/2 distinct parameters to estimate — for 500 stocks, that's over 125,000 numbers. If the number of historical observations T used to estimate Σ is anywhere near or below N, the sample covariance matrix becomes singular (if T≤N) or merely very noisy, which is fatal for an optimizer that needs Σ⁻¹ directly — a singular matrix can't even be inverted. Beyond the dimensionality problem, expected returns (μ) are themselves notoriously hard to estimate accurately, and small errors in μ can swing the resulting 'optimal' weights dramatically, which is one of the most cited practical criticisms of running the pure Markowitz framework unmodified.
questions.professionalAnswer: The dimensionality issue is the one I'd walk through with actual numbers, because it makes the problem concrete instead of abstract — with 500 stocks and maybe 100-250 days of usable recent data, you're trying to estimate well over 100,000 covariance terms from a fraction of that many observations, and the math just doesn't work; the matrix comes out singular or so noisy it's unusable. That's exactly why nobody running a large optimizer in practice uses the raw sample covariance matrix — they use a factor model or some form of shrinkage to collapse the estimation problem down to something the data can actually support.
commonMistakes: Only discussing the expected-return estimation problem and ignoring the covariance dimensionality problem
Not recognizing that a singular covariance matrix can't be inverted at all, which the optimizer directly needs
Assuming more historical data always fixes the problem, ignoring that very old data may not reflect current risk structure
Failing to mention factor models or shrinkage as the standard practical fixes
keyPoints: Mean-variance optimization needs expected returns (μ) and a full covariance matrix (Σ)
Σ has N(N+1)/2 parameters, growing roughly with the square of the number of assets
A singular or near-singular sample covariance matrix is unusable for optimization (can't invert)
Expected return estimation error is a separate, equally serious practical limitation

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes the required inputs (mu, Sigma)
Quantifies the dimensionality problem (N(N+1)/2 parameters)
Explains the singularity/invertibility consequence
Mentions expected-return estimation error as a related issue

questions.title: Explaining Why a Winning Year Still Needs Attribution
questions.prompt: Your portfolio manager says, 'We're up 14% this year, why do we need performance attribution?' How do you respond?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd explain that a healthy-looking total return can hide a losing position being masked by an unrelated winner — a portfolio's overall number tells you how much was made, but not where it actually came from, and you can't decide whether to keep, resize, or cut a given position or sleeve without knowing its real contribution. I'd walk through that a position's contribution to return is its weight times its own return, not its own return in isolation, so a position with a great individual return but a tiny allocation can contribute almost nothing, while a mediocre-returning position with a large allocation can dominate the number. I'd also note that attribution separates allocation effect (sector/asset-class weighting decisions) from selection effect (which specific names were picked), which tells us which type of decision is actually driving performance — information we need regardless of whether the headline number is good or bad.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the PM: a good year is exactly when you most want to know this, because it's the easiest time for a real problem to hide. If one position lost us 8 points and another made us 15, the 14% headline feels great, but we'd be sitting on a position that's been bleeding the whole time with nobody asking why. I'd rather surface that in a quiet, winning year than find out about it the first time a down year comes along and that same position is still dragging.
commonMistakes: Treating attribution as only useful when performance is bad
Conflating a position's own return with its contribution to the total portfolio return
Not distinguishing allocation effect from selection effect when explaining the value of attribution
Giving a vague 'it's best practice' answer without a concrete, PM-relevant reason
keyPoints: A positive total return can mask a losing position offset by a winner
Contribution to return = weight × return, not the position's own return alone
Attribution separates allocation effect from selection effect
Attribution is a diagnostic tool needed in good years as much as bad ones

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains the masking problem with a concrete mechanism
Correctly distinguishes contribution from standalone return
References allocation vs. selection effect
Delivers the point in PM-appropriate, constructive language

questions.title: A Trader Pushes Back on Your VaR Number
questions.prompt: A trader tells you your parametric VaR estimate 'feels too low' for their book. How do you respond, and what would actually make you reconsider the number?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd first ask the trader what specifically feels wrong — a gut sense, a recent loss that exceeded the number, or a specific exposure they don't think the model is capturing — since that tells me whether this is a methodology gap or a genuine disagreement about the risk. I'd walk through how the parametric VaR was built: it assumes normally distributed returns, which understates risk for a book with fat tails, skewed positions (like short options), or recent regime changes the historical window hasn't caught up to yet. I'd be honest that parametric VaR has real, well-known blind spots, and I'd offer to cross-check it against a historical simulation or Monte Carlo estimate on the same book — if those come out meaningfully higher, that's a legitimate reason to reconsider the number and potentially switch methodologies for this book specifically, rather than just asserting the original estimate is right.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't get defensive about this — a trader's gut feel about their own book is actually useful information, not just noise to dismiss. I'd ask them to be specific about what they think is missing, then go check it against a different VaR method on the same positions. If the parametric number is assuming normality on a book that's short gamma or has a lot of tail exposure, the trader's instinct is probably right, and historical or Monte Carlo VaR will usually show it. I'd rather find that out together than insist on the first number I handed them.
commonMistakes: Dismissing the trader's pushback without investigating the specific concern
Defending parametric VaR as definitively correct rather than acknowledging its known assumptions and blind spots
Not proposing a concrete cross-check (e.g., historical simulation or Monte Carlo) to validate or refute the concern
Changing the number just because the trader is unhappy, without an actual methodological basis
keyPoints: Ask what specifically feels wrong before responding — fat tails, skew, or a specific missed exposure
Parametric VaR assumes normal returns, which can understate risk for skewed or tail-heavy positions
A concrete cross-check against historical simulation or Monte Carlo VaR is the right way to validate concerns
Only revise the number based on a methodological finding, not social pressure alone

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Responds collaboratively rather than defensively
Correctly identifies parametric VaR's normality assumption as a plausible gap
Proposes a concrete cross-check methodology
States a clear, principled basis for when to actually revise the number

questions.title: Recommending a Hedge to a Non-Technical Stakeholder
questions.prompt: You've determined a portfolio needs a delta-hedge adjustment and a futures overlay to manage currency exposure. How do you explain this recommendation to a stakeholder who doesn't know what 'delta' means?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd translate each piece into what it does rather than how it's computed: the delta-hedge adjustment means our options position has become more sensitive to the stock's price than it was when we first put it on, so we need to buy or sell some additional shares to bring that sensitivity back down to roughly neutral — otherwise a normal day's stock move could swing our P&L more than intended. The currency futures overlay means a portion of our exposure is really a bet on the exchange rate, not on the investment itself, so we're using a futures contract to offset that currency risk and isolate the actual investment decision we want to be making. I'd close by stating the expected effect in dollar or percentage terms — 'this reduces our exposure to a 1% move in the stock/currency by roughly X' — since that's the number that actually matters to a non-technical stakeholder.
questions.professionalAnswer: I try to never say the word 'delta' to someone who hasn't asked for it directly — I'll describe the effect instead: 'our position's sensitivity to the stock has drifted up since we put the hedge on, so we need to true it back up,' and for the currency piece, 'about a fifth of our risk right now is really just a currency bet we didn't intend to make, and this overlay removes most of that.' If they want the mechanics I'll go deeper, but I lead with what changes for them, not with the Greek letters.

Failing to quantify the expected impact in terms the stakeholder cares about
Treating the two hedges (equity delta and currency overlay) as one undifferentiated concept
Over-simplifying to the point of being inaccurate about what the hedge actually does

questions.title: GARCH(1,1) Persistence and the Stationarity Condition
questions.prompt: A fitted GARCH(1,1) model produces alpha=0.08 and beta=0.90. Interpret what alpha and beta each mean here, confirm whether the process is stationary, and explain what a high beta implies about how long volatility shocks persist.
questions.code:
sigma_t^2 = omega + alpha*eps_(t-1)^2 + beta*sigma_(t-1)^2
Stationarity requires alpha + beta < 1
questions.modelAnswer: Alpha (0.08) measures how strongly a fresh shock moves today's conditional variance — a larger recent squared return shock has a direct, immediate effect on volatility. Beta (0.90) measures persistence — how much of yesterday's variance carries forward into today's. Checking stationarity: alpha + beta = 0.08 + 0.90 = 0.98, which is less than 1, so the process is (covariance) stationary with a well-defined long-run average variance. A beta this high (0.85-0.95 is common in real equity data) means volatility shocks decay slowly — a turbulent event can leave the market elevated and jumpy for a long stretch afterward, since 90% of each day's variance level is carried into the next, before mean-reverting very gradually toward the long-run average.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always check alpha + beta against 1 first, since that single number tells you whether the model is even well-behaved — here it's 0.98, comfortably stationary but close enough to 1 that I'd flag this as a highly persistent volatility regime. A beta of 0.90 specifically tells me that shocks fade out slowly; I wouldn't expect volatility to snap back to its long-run average quickly after a spike, which matters directly for how far out a risk forecast should be trusted.
commonMistakes: Confusing which coefficient (alpha vs. beta) measures shock sensitivity versus persistence
Forgetting to check alpha + beta < 1 before trusting the model's long-run behavior
Assuming a high beta means volatility never mean-reverts, rather than that it mean-reverts slowly
Treating alpha + beta close to 1 as automatically a modeling error rather than a real feature of persistent markets
keyPoints: Alpha measures the immediate sensitivity of variance to a fresh shock
Beta measures the persistence of past variance into today's conditional variance
Stationarity requires alpha + beta < 1, with a well-defined long-run average variance
A high beta means shocks decay slowly, not that they never decay

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly interprets alpha and beta separately
Correctly checks and confirms the stationarity condition
Correctly explains the persistence implication of a high beta

questions.title: Computing a One-Step-Ahead GARCH Variance Forecast
questions.prompt: A GARCH(1,1) model has omega=0.000002, alpha=0.08, beta=0.90. Yesterday's squared return shock was 0.0004 and yesterday's conditional variance was 0.00025. Compute today's forecast conditional variance and convert it to an annualized volatility.
questions.code:
sigma_t^2 = omega + alpha*eps_(t-1)^2 + beta*sigma_(t-1)^2
annualized_vol = sqrt(sigma_t^2 * 252)
questions.modelAnswer: sigma_t^2 = 0.000002 + 0.08*0.0004 + 0.90*0.00025 = 0.000002 + 0.000032 + 0.000225 = 0.000259. Daily volatility = sqrt(0.000259) ≈ 0.01609, or about 1.61%. Annualized volatility = 0.01609 * sqrt(252) ≈ 0.01609 * 15.87 ≈ 0.2554, or about 25.5%. This forecast sits close to yesterday's variance since beta dominates the equation, consistent with a highly persistent GARCH process.
questions.professionalAnswer: I plug the three terms in one at a time rather than all at once, so I can sanity-check that beta's contribution dominates — it should, given beta=0.90 versus alpha=0.08. Here the forecast variance (0.000259) lands just above yesterday's own variance (0.00025), which makes sense since yesterday's shock was a bit larger than its recent typical level. Annualizing at the end is just multiplying the daily vol by sqrt(252), a step I never skip since the raw daily number is easy to misread as a percentage on its own.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to include the omega term in the forecast
Using today's variance instead of yesterday's as the beta term's input
Annualizing the variance directly instead of first taking its square root to get daily volatility
Forgetting the sqrt(252) scaling when converting daily to annualized volatility
keyPoints: The GARCH(1,1) forecast combines a constant, a shock term, and a persistence term
Beta's term typically dominates when beta is large relative to alpha
Daily variance must be square-rooted before annualizing, not annualized directly
Annualized volatility = daily volatility * sqrt(252)

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes the forecast conditional variance
Correctly converts to daily volatility
Correctly annualizes using sqrt(252)

questions.title: Why Realized Volatility Is Statistically More Efficient
questions.prompt: Explain precisely why using intraday 5-minute returns to compute a day's realized volatility produces a statistically more efficient estimate than using a single close-to-close daily return — and name a practical limitation of the realized volatility approach.
questions.code: RV_t = sqrt( sum_(j=1 to m) r_(t,j)^2 )
questions.modelAnswer: A single daily return gives exactly one observation per day to estimate that day's volatility, which inherently carries substantial sampling noise. Realized volatility instead sums squared intraday returns across m intervals (e.g., 78 five-minute bars in a 6.5-hour trading day), using far more data points to estimate the same single day's underlying volatility, which reduces the estimator's variance and produces a sharper, less noisy measurement — this is the same statistical principle behind why averaging over more observations shrinks estimation error. The practical limitation is market microstructure noise: at very high frequency, bid-ask bounce and other microstructure effects inflate the measured variance in a way that isn't genuine price volatility, so realized volatility estimates can become biased upward if the sampling frequency is pushed too high (too many intervals) relative to the asset's actual liquidity, which is why practitioners pick an intermediate frequency (like 5-minute bars) rather than the highest frequency available.
questions.professionalAnswer: The efficiency argument is really just 'more data points, same underlying quantity, less noise' — intuitively identical to why a sample mean of 80 observations is more reliable than one of 2. But I wouldn't push the sampling frequency as high as possible just because more data sounds better; at tick-level or even 1-minute frequency, bid-ask bounce starts contaminating the measurement, so there's a practical sweet spot, and 5-minute bars are a common, defensible choice precisely because they're fine enough to be efficient but coarse enough to avoid most microstructure noise.
commonMistakes: Assuming higher sampling frequency is always strictly better for realized volatility
Not naming market microstructure noise as the specific limitation at very high frequency
Confusing realized volatility's statistical efficiency with it being a volatility forecast rather than a measurement
Forgetting that realized volatility still requires annualizing for comparison across assets or methods
keyPoints: Realized volatility uses many intraday observations instead of one daily observation, reducing estimator variance
More observations per day produces a statistically sharper measurement of that day's true volatility
Market microstructure noise (e.g., bid-ask bounce) inflates measured variance at excessively high sampling frequency
Practitioners pick an intermediate frequency (e.g., 5-minute bars) to balance efficiency against microstructure noise

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the statistical efficiency argument
Correctly identifies microstructure noise as the practical limitation
Notes the need to balance frequency against this limitation

questions.title: Computing VaR From a GARCH Volatility Forecast
questions.prompt: A GARCH model forecasts tomorrow's daily volatility at 2.1%, and the position's expected daily return (mu) is approximately zero. Compute the 1-day 95% Value at Risk for a $10 million position, assuming normally distributed returns.
questions.code:
VaR_alpha = -(mu + z_alpha * sigma)
z_0.05 ~= -1.645
questions.modelAnswer: VaR_0.05 = -(0 + (-1.645)*0.021) = -(-0.03455) = 0.03455, or about 3.455% of the position. For a $10 million position, that's approximately $345,500. Interpretation: there's roughly a 5% chance that tomorrow's loss on this position exceeds about $345,500, based on the GARCH-forecast volatility rather than a flat historical standard deviation — this lets the VaR estimate adapt to current conditions (rising ahead of turbulent periods) rather than only reacting to volatility after the fact.
questions.professionalAnswer: I plug mu and the GARCH forecast straight into the formula, and I always double-check the sign convention — z_0.05 is negative, and the formula's leading negative sign flips it back to a positive loss number, which trips people up constantly. The real value of feeding a GARCH forecast in here instead of a flat historical sigma is that the VaR number moves with current market conditions, not just history.
commonMistakes: Mishandling the sign of z_alpha and arriving at a negative VaR figure
Using a flat historical volatility instead of the GARCH forecast, missing the point of the exercise
Forgetting to scale the percentage VaR by the position's dollar size
Assuming VaR here represents the worst possible loss rather than a 95% confidence threshold
keyPoints: VaR_alpha = -(mu + z_alpha * sigma), with z_alpha negative for a left-tail confidence level
A GARCH-based sigma lets VaR adapt to current volatility conditions, not just historical averages
VaR here is a 95% confidence threshold, not a maximum possible loss
The percentage VaR must be scaled by position size to get a dollar figure

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes the percentage VaR
Correctly scales to the dollar VaR figure
Correctly interprets the result as a 95% threshold, not a worst case

questions.title: Designing a Volatility-Targeting Overlay
questions.prompt: Design a volatility-targeting rule for a single-asset strategy that currently holds a fixed 100% notional position, with a target annualized risk level of 10%. Walk through how the position size would respond if the GARCH-forecast annualized volatility moved from 15% to 30%.
questions.modelAnswer: A volatility-targeting rule scales position size as target_vol / forecast_vol, rather than holding a fixed notional. With a 10% target and a 15% forecast, the position scales to 10/15 ≈ 0.667, or 66.7% notional — already below the fixed 100% because current volatility exceeds target. If the GARCH forecast then rises to 30%, the position rescales to 10/30 ≈ 0.333, or 33.3% notional — roughly half of its prior size, cutting exposure as volatility doubles so the position's expected risk contribution stays close to the 10% target throughout, rather than passively doubling in risk alongside the market. This requires rebalancing the position whenever the volatility forecast updates meaningfully, which introduces its own turnover and transaction cost tradeoff worth weighing against the risk-control benefit.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build it as a simple ratio — target over forecast — and let that ratio directly scale the notional, recomputed each time the volatility forecast updates. The behavior under a vol doubling (15% to 30%) is exactly what you want to see: the position roughly halves, which is the entire point of the overlay — it's actively managing risk exposure instead of letting the market dictate how much risk the book is carrying on any given day. I'd also flag the turnover cost of frequent rebalancing as a real design tradeoff, not a footnote.
commonMistakes: Scaling position size directly by the volatility forecast instead of inversely
Not recomputing the scaling ratio when the underlying volatility forecast updates
Ignoring the transaction cost and turnover implications of frequent rebalancing
Confusing volatility targeting with simply avoiding the asset when volatility rises
keyPoints: Position size scales as target_vol / forecast_vol, inversely with forecast volatility
A doubling of forecast volatility roughly halves the position size under this rule
The goal is to hold expected risk contribution roughly constant over time
Rebalancing frequency introduces a turnover/cost tradeoff against the risk-control benefit

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly specifies the inverse-volatility scaling rule
Correctly computes the position size at both volatility levels

questions.title: The Fama-French Five-Factor Extension
questions.prompt: What do RMW and CMA add to the Fama-French three-factor model, and why did adding them change how much credit HML gets for explaining returns?
questions.code: R_i - R_f = alpha + b_mkt*(R_m-R_f) + b_smb*SMB + b_hml*HML + b_rmw*RMW + b_cma*CMA + eps
questions.modelAnswer: RMW ('Robust Minus Weak') is a long-short factor long firms with high operating profitability and short firms with low profitability; CMA ('Conservative Minus Aggressive') is long firms investing conservatively (low asset growth) and short firms investing aggressively (high asset growth). Both are constructed the same long-short way as SMB and HML. Adding them explains more of the cross-section of average returns largely because profitability and investment patterns were previously getting folded into HML's value signal — a 'cheap' stock by book-to-market is often cheap partly because it's less profitable or growing more aggressively, so HML was implicitly picking up some of what RMW and CMA now measure directly. Once RMW and CMA are added as separate factors, HML's own loadings and explanatory contribution typically shrink, because some of what it used to 'get credit for' is now attributed to the two new, more specific factors.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd describe RMW and CMA as the five-factor model's way of unbundling what HML was doing all along — a lot of 'value' as measured by book-to-market was really a mix of profitability and investment-intensity signals wearing a value costume. Once you separate those out explicitly, HML's measured contribution naturally shrinks, not because value stopped mattering, but because the model got more precise about what was actually driving the pattern.
commonMistakes: Describing RMW and CMA without specifying which side of each long-short pair is long vs. short
Not explaining why HML's explanatory power changes once RMW and CMA are added
Treating the five-factor model as simply 'more factors are always better' without the mechanistic reason
Confusing RMW/CMA's construction method with a different estimation technique than SMB/HML
keyPoints: RMW: long high-profitability firms, short low-profitability firms
CMA: long conservative-investment firms, short aggressive-investment firms
Both are constructed as long-short portfolios, exactly like SMB and HML
Adding them reduces HML's apparent explanatory power by unbundling profitability/investment effects it was implicitly capturing

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly defines RMW and CMA
Correctly explains why HML's contribution shrinks after adding them

questions.title: Recovering Factor Loadings via OLS
questions.prompt: You regress a fund's monthly excess returns on the market, SMB, and HML factors and get: alpha = 0.0003 (t-stat 0.6), beta_mkt = 1.10, beta_smb = 0.35, beta_hml = -0.20, R-squared = 0.81. What does this tell you about the fund's actual sources of return, and is the fund's manager demonstrating real skill?
questions.code: R_i - R_f = alpha + b_mkt*(R_m-R_f) + b_smb*SMB + b_hml*HML + eps
questions.modelAnswer: The high R-squared (0.81) means 81% of the fund's return variance is explained by just these three factor exposures, leaving only 19% unexplained by factor exposure. The loadings describe the fund's actual tilts: beta_mkt=1.10 means it runs somewhat more market exposure than the index itself, beta_smb=0.35 means a meaningful tilt toward small-cap-like behavior, and beta_hml=-0.20 means a growth tilt (negative value exposure) rather than a value tilt. The alpha of 0.0003 with a t-stat of only 0.6 is statistically indistinguishable from zero — far below the conventional threshold (typically |t| > 2) for significance. The conclusion: most of what this fund delivers is explained by its factor tilts (size, market, and growth-style exposure), not by manager skill beyond those exposures — an investor could largely replicate this fund's behavior with cheap factor-tilted index exposure rather than paying for active management.
questions.professionalAnswer: The R-squared of 0.81 is the number I'd lead with — that's a huge share of the return explained by exposure alone, before I even look at alpha. And the alpha's t-stat of 0.6 confirms it: there's no statistically meaningful skill showing up here once the market, size, and value/growth tilts are accounted for. I'd tell an allocator this fund is largely a factor-tilted product, and the real question is whether they're being charged active-management fees for something closer to a systematic factor exposure.

questions.title: Time-Series Regression vs Cross-Sectional Regression
questions.prompt: What's the difference between a time-series regression and a cross-sectional regression in factor analysis, and why does each one answer a fundamentally different question?
questions.code:
Time-series: fix one asset, regress across many periods -> estimates beta_i
Cross-sectional: fix one period, regress across many assets -> estimates lambda (price of risk)
questions.modelAnswer: A time-series regression fixes one asset and uses many time periods, regressing that asset's returns on a factor over time — this estimates the asset's beta, answering 'how sensitive is this specific asset to the factor.' A cross-sectional regression instead fixes one time period and regresses the returns of many assets on their betas at that moment — this estimates the risk premium (lambda), answering a completely different question: 'is this factor exposure actually compensated with extra return, and by how much, across the market at this point in time.' Both regressions are necessary for a complete picture: the time-series step tells you how exposed each asset is, and the cross-sectional step tells you whether that exposure is being paid for at all.
questions.professionalAnswer: I keep these straight by asking what's fixed and what varies: time-series fixes the asset and varies time, cross-sectional fixes time and varies the asset. One tells you an asset's exposure; the other tells you the market's going rate for that exposure. Mixing them up — or not realizing they're answering different questions — is a common source of confused interpretation when someone just says 'I ran a factor regression' without specifying which kind.

Assuming a time-series regression tells you anything about whether a factor is compensated
Assuming a cross-sectional regression tells you about one specific asset's exposure
Not recognizing both regressions are typically needed together for a complete risk-premium analysis
keyPoints: Time-series regression: one asset, many periods, estimates that asset's beta
Cross-sectional regression: one period, many assets, estimates the factor's price of risk (lambda)
Time-series answers 'how exposed is this asset'; cross-sectional answers 'is this exposure compensated'
Both steps together form the basis of the Fama-MacBeth procedure

questions.title: Why a Naive Cross-Sectional Regression Understates Risk-Premium Uncertainty
questions.prompt: A colleague estimates each asset's beta once from history, then runs a single cross-sectional regression of average returns on those betas, reporting a tight standard error on the resulting risk premium. What's wrong with trusting that standard error?
questions.modelAnswer: This single naive cross-sectional regression suffers from the errors-in-variables problem: the betas used as regressors are themselves estimates with their own sampling error, not the true unobserved betas, and that estimation error biases the resulting slope (classically toward zero) and makes the standard error from that one regression unreliable. A deeper issue compounds this: treating each asset as an independent observation in a single cross-sectional regression ignores that asset returns are correlated with each other within the same period — which overstates the regression's effective sample size and produces an artificially tight standard error. The correct fix is the Fama-MacBeth procedure: run a separate cross-sectional regression in each time period, then build the standard error from how much the resulting risk-premium estimate (lambda_t) actually varies across periods, which captures the real sampling uncertainty rather than a falsely precise single-regression number.
questions.professionalAnswer: The tight standard error is the giveaway here — it's almost always too good to be true in a naive single cross-sectional regression, because it's quietly treating each of (say) 60 correlated assets as 60 independent data points. I'd immediately suggest running Fama-MacBeth instead: many smaller cross-sectional regressions, one per period, with the standard error coming from how much the risk premium bounces around across those periods — that's a far more honest number, even though it's usually several times larger.

Treating correlated assets within one period as independent observations
Not proposing Fama-MacBeth as the standard correction

questions.title: Designing a Fama-MacBeth Estimation
questions.prompt: You need to report an honest risk-premium estimate and standard error for a factor across 240 months of data on 60 assets. Walk through the three steps of the Fama-MacBeth procedure you'd implement, and explain what makes its standard error more trustworthy than a single-shot regression's.
questions.code:
lambda_FM = mean(lambda_1, ..., lambda_T)
SE(lambda_FM) = std(lambda_1, ..., lambda_T) / sqrt(T)
questions.modelAnswer: Step 1 (time-series): for each of the 60 assets, run a time-series regression of its returns on the factor across all 240 months to estimate that asset's beta. Step 2 (cross-sectional): for each of the 240 months, run a cross-sectional regression of that month's returns across all 60 assets on the step-1 betas, producing one risk-premium estimate (lambda_t) per month. Step 3 (average and standard error): the final risk-premium estimate is the mean of the 240 lambda_t values, and critically, its standard error is the standard deviation of the lambda_t series divided by sqrt(240) — treating each month as one observation, not each asset. This is more trustworthy than a single-shot regression because it measures real month-to-month variability in the risk-premium estimate directly, rather than implicitly assuming 60 independent observations per month when the assets' returns actually move together within each month — a risk premium that bounces around wildly from month to month correctly gets a large, honest standard error under this approach.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd build it exactly as the three steps suggest: betas once per asset over the full history, then one small cross-sectional regression per month, then treat the resulting 240 lambda values as the real sample whose variability defines the standard error. The key mental model is that each *month* is the unit of independent information here, not each asset-month combination — that's exactly why the standard error comes out larger and more honest than a naive single regression would suggest.

Computing the standard error from the asset-level dispersion rather than the period-level lambda_t series
Forgetting to divide by sqrt(T) when computing the final standard error
Not recognizing that each period, not each asset, is the unit of independent information in step 3

Step 2: per-period cross-sectional regression to estimate lambda_t
Step 3: average the lambda_t values; standard error = std(lambda_t) / sqrt(T)

questions.title: Why a 500-Stock Sample Covariance Matrix Breaks Down
questions.prompt: A quant team tries to estimate a full sample covariance matrix for 500 stocks using 200 days of historical returns, and the optimizer that depends on it fails. What exactly goes wrong, numerically, and why?
questions.code: Free parameters in Sigma = N*(N+1)/2
questions.modelAnswer: A 500-asset covariance matrix has N*(N+1)/2 = 500*501/2 = 125,250 distinct parameters to estimate (variances plus unique covariances). With only 200 historical observations — fewer than the number of assets (N=500 > T=200) — the sample covariance matrix becomes mathematically singular: it cannot have more than T=200 independent directions of variance, so at least 300 of its eigenvalues come out as exactly or numerically zero. A singular matrix cannot be inverted, and mean-variance optimization needs Sigma^(-1) directly, so the optimization fails outright rather than merely producing a noisy answer. This isn't a matter of the data being 'a little thin' — it's a hard mathematical wall: you cannot estimate more independent variance directions than you have independent observations.
questions.professionalAnswer: The moment I hear 'more assets than observations,' I already know the sample covariance matrix is going to be singular before I even run anything — that's just a fact about rank, not a data-quality issue you can fix by being more careful. I'd explain it to the team in exactly those terms: you're asking for over 125,000 numbers from 200 data points, and the matrix mathematically cannot have more rank than the smaller of those two numbers.
commonMistakes: Describing the problem as the estimate being 'noisy' rather than mathematically singular
Not computing the actual parameter count (N*(N+1)/2) to make the scale of the problem concrete
Assuming more historical data always fixes the problem regardless of how much more is needed
Not connecting the singularity directly to the optimizer's need for Sigma inverse
keyPoints: A covariance matrix for N assets has N*(N+1)/2 free parameters
A sample covariance matrix is singular whenever the number of observations T <= N
A singular matrix has zero eigenvalues and cannot be inverted
Mean-variance optimization requires Sigma inverse directly, so singularity causes outright failure

questions.title: Switching to a Factor-Model Covariance Matrix
questions.prompt: Design a practical fix for the singular-covariance-matrix problem on a 500-stock universe with limited history, using a factor-model approach. What does the resulting covariance matrix look like structurally, and why does it solve the dimensionality problem?
questions.code: Sigma = B * Sigma_F * B' + D
questions.modelAnswer: Instead of estimating every pairwise covariance directly, assume each asset's return is driven by a small number k of common factors plus idiosyncratic noise. The covariance matrix then decomposes as Sigma = B * Sigma_F * B' + D, where B is the N x k matrix of factor loadings (estimated once per asset by regression), Sigma_F is the small k x k covariance matrix of the factors themselves, and D is a diagonal matrix of idiosyncratic variances (assumed uncorrelated across assets). This collapses the estimation problem from N*(N+1)/2 free parameters down to roughly N*k (loadings) plus k*(k+1)/2 (factor covariance) plus N (idiosyncratic variances) — for 500 assets and 3 factors, that's on the order of a few thousand parameters instead of over 125,000. The resulting matrix is automatically full rank and invertible, because the added diagonal idiosyncratic term guarantees every eigenvalue is strictly positive, solving the dimensionality problem at the cost of assuming the factor structure is a reasonably good description of how returns actually co-move.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd pitch this as trading a problem you can't solve for one you can, by making a reasonable assumption: that most of the co-movement between 500 stocks flows through a handful of common factors, not 125,000 independent relationships. Structurally, B*Sigma_F*B' plus a diagonal D is the whole fix — that diagonal term alone is what guarantees the matrix is invertible, since it keeps every eigenvalue strictly positive no matter how thin the factor structure's own estimate is.
commonMistakes: Not naming the specific decomposition Sigma = B*Sigma_F*B' + D
Forgetting that the diagonal idiosyncratic term is what guarantees invertibility
Not quantifying how dramatically the factor-model approach reduces the parameter count
Treating the factor-model covariance as risk-free or exact rather than an approximation with its own assumptions
keyPoints: Sigma = B * Sigma_F * B' + D, with B the loadings, Sigma_F the factor covariance, D the idiosyncratic diagonal
This reduces parameters from N*(N+1)/2 to roughly N*k + k*(k+1)/2 + N
The diagonal D term guarantees full rank and invertibility

Correctly explains the parameter-count reduction

questions.title: Diagnosing a Pairs Trade That's Correlated But Not Cointegrated
questions.prompt: A pairs trade between two energy stocks shows a 0.92 historical correlation but has been losing money steadily for six months as the spread drifts wider instead of reverting. Walk through exactly how you'd test whether this pair was ever a legitimate statistical arbitrage candidate.
questions.code: Engle-Granger: regress log_a on log_b, test residual (spread) for stationarity via ADF
questions.modelAnswer: I'd run the Engle-Granger two-step test directly: regress one stock's log price on the other's to estimate the hedge ratio, then test the resulting residual (the spread) for stationarity using an Augmented Dickey-Fuller test. If the ADF test fails to reject a unit root (i.e., the spread is not stationary), that confirms the pair was never actually cointegrated — the 0.92 correlation was measuring co-movement over the sample, not a genuine mean-reverting relationship, and two trending-together-but-not-cointegrated series can easily drift apart permanently. The continued widening over six months with no reversion is itself consistent with exactly this diagnosis: a spread with no real long-run equilibrium to revert to. The fix going forward is to require a passing cointegration test, not just a correlation threshold, before putting on a pairs trade — and to re-test periodically, since even a genuinely cointegrating relationship can break down (a merger, a diverging business model) and needs ongoing validation, not a one-time check.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd go straight to the ADF test on the regression residual rather than re-examining the correlation number, because correlation was never the right test in the first place. If the ADF test doesn't reject a unit root, that's the answer right there — this spread has no statistical tendency to revert, and six months of steady widening is exactly the symptom you'd expect from that diagnosis, not bad luck.
commonMistakes: Re-checking the correlation coefficient instead of running an actual cointegration test
Assuming a high correlation alone was ever sufficient justification for the original trade
Not recognizing that even a genuinely cointegrated pair needs periodic re-validation
Confusing the Engle-Granger residual test with simply checking if the spread 'looks' mean-reverting on a chart
keyPoints: The Engle-Granger test regresses one series on the other, then tests the residual spread for stationarity
A failing ADF test (can't reject a unit root) means the pair was never cointegrated
High correlation without cointegration explains persistent, non-reverting spread widening
Cointegration should be tested before the trade and periodically re-validated afterward

Correctly connects a failing test to the observed symptom
Recommends ongoing re-validation, not just a one-time check

questions.title: Building a Pairs Trade's Hedge Ratio and Z-Score
questions.prompt: Given two cointegrated stocks' log prices, walk through how you'd estimate the hedge ratio, construct the spread, and turn it into entry and exit signals using a z-score. What does 'long the spread' actually mean as a set of trades?
questions.code:
beta, intercept = polyfit(log_b, log_a, deg=1)
spread = log_a - beta * log_b
zscore = (spread - spread.rolling(window).mean()) / spread.rolling(window).std()
questions.modelAnswer: First, estimate the hedge ratio beta via OLS regression of log_a on log_b (log_a = beta*log_b + intercept) — beta says how many units of asset B offset one unit of asset A. Build the spread as spread = log_a - beta*log_b. Then compute a rolling z-score of the spread: (spread - rolling_mean) / rolling_std, shifted by one period to avoid lookahead. Entry/exit rules: enter 'long the spread' when the z-score drops below a negative threshold (e.g., -2), enter 'short the spread' when it rises above a positive threshold (+2), and close out when the z-score returns near zero (e.g., within 0.5). 'Long the spread' concretely means long asset A and short beta units of asset B — betting the spread will widen back toward its mean from below; 'short the spread' means the opposite position, betting it narrows back from above. Both legs trade together; neither is held in isolation.
questions.professionalAnswer: I build it in the same order every time: estimate beta via regression, form the spread, z-score it on a rolling window with a lag to avoid lookahead, then apply symmetric entry and exit thresholds. 'Long the spread' trips people up until they see it written as two simultaneous trades — long A, short beta*B — rather than a single position; once that clicks, the entry/exit logic around the z-score is straightforward.
questions.example: beta estimated via OLS; spread = log_a - beta*log_b; enter long when zscore < -2, enter short when zscore > 2, exit when |zscore| < 0.5.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to shift the z-score by at least one period before generating signals
Describing 'long the spread' as a single position rather than two simultaneous legs
Using a static hedge ratio estimated once and never re-estimated on a rolling basis
Setting entry and exit thresholds without checking they're symmetric and consistent
keyPoints: Hedge ratio beta is estimated via OLS regression between the two log price series
Spread = log_a - beta * log_b
Z-score of the spread, shifted to avoid lookahead, drives entry and exit signals
'Long the spread' means long A and short beta units of B simultaneously

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly describes hedge ratio estimation
Correctly describes spread and z-score construction
Correctly describes entry/exit threshold logic
Correctly explains what 'long the spread' means as two legs

questions.title: A Momentum Strategy Hit by a Momentum Crash
questions.prompt: A 12-1 month momentum strategy has performed well for two years, then loses a large share of its cumulative gains in a few weeks right as the market sharply reverses off a low. Explain the mechanism behind this specific failure, and what, if anything, could have been done differently in the strategy's construction.
questions.modelAnswer: This is a classic momentum crash: a momentum strategy is, by construction, fully invested in whatever has recently outperformed, which typically means it's heavily long the stocks that fell the least (or rose the most) during a prior downturn and short the stocks that fell the most. When the market sharply reverses off a low, the prior losers (which the strategy is short) tend to rebound the hardest — exactly the stocks a momentum strategy is positioned against — producing outsized losses on both the long and short legs simultaneously. This is a well-documented pattern, especially around market turning points following a drawdown. Mitigations include capping position sizes or gross exposure during high-volatility regimes (since momentum crashes cluster with volatility spikes), incorporating a volatility-scaling overlay similar to a GARCH-based position-sizing rule, or blending momentum with an uncorrelated strategy family (like carry or mean reversion) whose own failure mode isn't triggered by the same market-turn event.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain the mechanism first, because it's not random bad luck — momentum crashes have a specific, well-documented trigger: the stocks you're short are usually the prior losers, and those are exactly the names that snap back hardest at a turning point. Once that's clear, the fix options are about reducing exposure specifically when conditions look crash-prone (elevated volatility, a market near a prior trough) rather than assuming the signal itself is broken.
commonMistakes: Describing the loss as random noise rather than the well-documented momentum-crash mechanism
Not explaining why the short leg specifically suffers at a market turning point
Proposing to abandon momentum entirely rather than adding risk controls specific to this failure mode
Not connecting the crash risk to elevated volatility as a warning signal
keyPoints: Momentum is fully invested in recent outperformers, short recent underperformers
A sharp reversal off a low causes prior losers (the short leg) to rebound hardest
Momentum crashes are a well-documented, structural failure mode, not random noise
Mitigations include volatility-based exposure scaling or blending with uncorrelated strategy families

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the momentum crash mechanism
Correctly identifies why the short leg specifically suffers
Proposes a reasonable mitigation
