questions.title: Explaining a Crowded Stat-Arb Unwind
questions.prompt: A 'market-neutral' statistical arbitrage book lost money sharply during a known historical event where many similar quant books were unwinding at once, even though none of its individual pairs' cointegrating relationships had actually broken. How do you explain this to a PM who's confused because 'nothing in the model was wrong'?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd explain that the model being 'right' about cointegration doesn't protect against a different, orthogonal risk: crowding. Many stat-arb desks tend to hold economically similar pairs and run similar styles of mean-reversion strategies. When several firms need to unwind similar positions at once — often triggered by one large fund's forced deleveraging, unrelated to any individual pair's own fundamentals — the resulting correlated selling can make normally low-volatility, well-behaved spreads move violently in a way no single pair's own history would have predicted. This is distinct from the cointegrating relationship breaking down; the statistical relationship between the two stocks may still be perfectly intact, but the trade still loses money because everyone holding similar positions is forced to exit simultaneously, pushing spreads temporarily (sometimes severely) against everyone at once.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the PM directly: the model wasn't wrong, the risk that hit us was never in the model at all. Crowding risk is about who else holds a position like yours, not about whether your own statistical relationship held up — and that's exactly why it blindsides books that did everything right on an individual-pair basis. I'd use this as the opening for a conversation about whether we need some explicit measure of crowding or positioning risk layered on top of our usual pair-by-pair diligence.
commonMistakes: Conflating crowding risk with the cointegrating relationship actually breaking down
Treating the loss as evidence the model or methodology was flawed
Not explaining the correlated, forced-unwind mechanism concretely
Failing to suggest a forward-looking response such as monitoring crowding or positioning risk
keyPoints: Crowding risk is distinct from a cointegrating relationship breaking down
Many stat-arb desks hold economically similar pairs and similar strategy styles
A forced, correlated unwind by other participants can move spreads violently with no change in the underlying relationship
This is a real, known risk (e.g., August 2007) that individual-pair diligence alone doesn't protect against

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly distinguishes crowding risk from a broken cointegrating relationship
Explains the correlated-unwind mechanism clearly
Communicates this constructively, with a forward-looking suggestion

questions.title: Continuous Kelly and Fractional Kelly in Practice
questions.prompt: A strategy has an estimated annualized mean return of 12% and annualized variance of 0.16 (standard deviation 40%). Compute the full continuous Kelly fraction, then the recommended fractional Kelly at a 0.5 scale-down, and explain why the full-Kelly number shouldn't be used directly.
questions.code: f* = mu / sigma^2
questions.modelAnswer: f* = 0.12 / 0.16 = 0.75, meaning full Kelly recommends sizing the position at 75% of capital. Fractional Kelly at 0.5 scale-down: 0.5 * 0.75 = 0.375, or 37.5% of capital. Full Kelly shouldn't be used directly for two compounding reasons: it maximizes long-run growth by accepting very large short-term swings, with drawdowns of 50% or more entirely possible even when the underlying edge is completely real; and mu here is itself an estimate with real sampling error — if the true mu is smaller than 12% (a very real possibility over any realistic sample length), the full-Kelly position is oversized relative to the actual edge, with no built-in awareness in the formula that mu might be wrong. Fractional Kelly directly hedges against both issues by giving up some long-run growth for a dramatically smoother ride and reduced sensitivity to mu being overestimated.
questions.professionalAnswer: 75% of capital on a single strategy sounds aggressive the moment you say it out loud, and that's exactly the instinct full Kelly should trigger — it's mathematically optimal for growth, but only if mu and sigma^2 are known exactly, which they never are. I'd default straight to the fractional version, 37.5% here, and treat that scale-down less as caution for its own sake and more as a direct, practical hedge against the very real chance that 12% is an overestimate of the true edge.
questions.example: f* = 0.12/0.16 = 0.75 (75% full Kelly). Fractional Kelly at 0.5x = 0.375 (37.5%).
commonMistakes: Forgetting to square sigma before dividing (using sigma instead of sigma^2)
Treating the full Kelly fraction as the actual recommended position size
Not connecting the fractional Kelly scale-down to the specific risk of mu being overestimated
Assuming fractional Kelly is just arbitrary conservatism rather than a targeted hedge against estimation error
keyPoints: Continuous Kelly: f* = mu / sigma^2, using annualized values
Full Kelly accepts large short-term drawdowns even with a genuinely real edge
mu is an estimate with real sampling error, and Kelly has no built-in awareness of that uncertainty
Fractional Kelly (commonly 0.25-0.5x) hedges directly against overestimating the true edge

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes the full Kelly fraction
Correctly computes the fractional Kelly fraction
Explains the drawdown risk of full Kelly
Explains the mu-estimation-error risk and fractional Kelly's role as a hedge against it

questions.title: Over-Levering a Noisy Kelly Estimate
questions.prompt: A strategy's backtest estimates mu and sigma^2 and computes a full Kelly fraction of 40% of capital. Instead of using fractional Kelly, the PM decides to apply 2x leverage on top of the full-Kelly sizing, reasoning that 'the math already tells us the optimal size, so leverage just scales up good decisions.' What's wrong with this reasoning, and how does it actually play out if the estimated edge was overstated?
questions.modelAnswer: This reasoning conflates 'mathematically optimal given known mu and sigma^2' with 'safe to lever further,' when the real risk is that mu and sigma^2 were never actually known — they were estimated from a finite, noisy backtest sample, and the Kelly formula has no built-in awareness of that uncertainty. If the true underlying mu is smaller than the backtest's estimate (a very real possibility, especially over a short sample), the already-computed 40% Kelly fraction was oversized relative to the real edge before any leverage was applied — and multiplying that overestimate by 2x doesn't scale up a good decision, it scales up the original estimation error along with it. In practice this compounds two separate problems at once: the sizing was wrong to begin with, and leverage now means a real decline toward the true (smaller) edge produces a much larger drawdown and a real risk of a margin call forcing an exit at the worst possible time — converting what should have been a modest sizing error into an account-threatening one.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd push back on the framing directly: the formula isn't telling you the optimal size, it's telling you the optimal size *if* mu and sigma^2 are exactly right, and they never are. Leveraging on top of an estimate, instead of scaling it down with fractional Kelly, takes whatever estimation error was already baked into the 40% number and doubles it — that's one of the most common, well-documented ways a quantitatively 'correct-looking' strategy ends up producing a real, account-ending loss.
commonMistakes: Treating a Kelly-derived sizing number as a known-safe quantity rather than an estimate with real uncertainty
Assuming leverage simply scales up a good outcome rather than scaling up the underlying estimation error
Not connecting the over-levering to the realistic risk of a forced margin-call exit
Recommending fractional Kelly only as general caution rather than as a specific hedge against this exact failure mode
keyPoints: Kelly's formula assumes mu and sigma^2 are known exactly, which they never are in practice
Leveraging a Kelly estimate scales up its estimation error, not just its correctness
If the true edge is smaller than estimated, leverage converts a sizing error into an account-threatening loss
Fractional Kelly, not added leverage, is the standard, specific defense against this risk

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly identifies the flaw in the PM's reasoning
Explains how leverage compounds estimation error rather than scaling a correct decision
Connects the risk to a realistic negative outcome (forced exit, outsized drawdown)

questions.title: Computing Marginal Risk Contribution
questions.prompt: A two-asset portfolio has weights w = [0.6, 0.4] and covariance matrix Sigma = [[0.04, 0.01], [0.01, 0.09]] (in variance units). Compute each asset's marginal contribution to risk and its percentage share of total portfolio risk.
questions.code:
portfolio_var = w' * Sigma * w
marginal_contrib = (Sigma @ w) / portfolio_vol
risk_contrib = w * marginal_contrib
questions.modelAnswer: First, Sigma @ w = [0.04*0.6 + 0.01*0.4, 0.01*0.6 + 0.09*0.4] = [0.024+0.004, 0.006+0.036] = [0.028, 0.042]. Portfolio variance = w' * (Sigma @ w) = 0.6*0.028 + 0.4*0.042 = 0.0168 + 0.0168 = 0.0336. Portfolio volatility = sqrt(0.0336) ≈ 0.1833. Marginal contribution = [0.028, 0.042] / 0.1833 ≈ [0.1527, 0.2292]. Risk contribution = w * marginal_contrib ≈ [0.6*0.1527, 0.4*0.2292] ≈ [0.0916, 0.0917], which sum to ≈0.1833 (matching portfolio volatility, as expected). As a percentage of total risk: Asset 1 ≈ 50.0%, Asset 2 ≈ 50.0% — despite Asset 1 having a 60% dollar weight, both assets contribute almost exactly equal shares of total portfolio risk, because Asset 2's higher individual variance (0.09 vs 0.04) offsets its smaller weight.
questions.professionalAnswer: I always compute Sigma @ w first as its own step, since it's reused in both the portfolio variance and the marginal contribution calculations. The result here is the kind of thing risk budgeting is built to catch: a 60/40 dollar split looks balanced on paper, but the actual risk split comes out close to 50/50 once Asset 2's higher volatility is accounted for — dollar weight and risk weight are simply not the same thing.
questions.example: Sigma@w = [0.028, 0.042]. Portfolio vol ≈ 0.1833. Risk contributions ≈ [0.0916, 0.0917] → roughly 50%/50% despite 60%/40% dollar weights.
commonMistakes: Computing marginal contribution without first taking the square root to get portfolio volatility from variance
Forgetting that risk contributions should sum to total portfolio volatility, not variance
Assuming dollar weight automatically equals risk weight
Mixing up the order of the matrix-vector multiplication Sigma @ w
keyPoints: Portfolio variance = w' * Sigma * w; portfolio vol is its square root
Marginal contribution to risk = (Sigma @ w) / portfolio_vol
Risk contribution = weight * marginal contribution, summing to total portfolio volatility
Dollar weight and risk-contribution share can differ substantially when volatilities differ

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes Sigma @ w and portfolio variance/volatility
Correctly computes marginal contribution to risk
Correctly computes and interprets the percentage risk contributions

questions.title: Designing Gross Exposure Limits for a Long-Short Book
questions.prompt: You're setting risk limits for a new long-short equity book. The PM wants maximum flexibility to run high gross exposure as long as net exposure stays near zero. What financing and risk considerations should shape the gross exposure limit, independent of net exposure?
questions.modelAnswer: Net-neutral doesn't make gross exposure free: every dollar of gross exposure still carries financing costs (borrowing costs on the short leg, margin interest on the long leg) that compound as gross rises, directly eating into returns regardless of net market exposure. Gross exposure also directly drives margin requirements set by the prime broker, which can tighten suddenly in stressed markets, forcing deleveraging at the worst possible time. Most importantly, high gross exposure amplifies correlation-breakdown risk: if the long and short legs' correlation unexpectedly weakens (as covered in the correlation-to-one discussion), a book running 400% gross with 0% net can still suffer losses many times larger than one running 150% gross with the same 0% net, because there's simply far more notional exposed on each side when the hedge stops working as expected. A sensible gross limit should be set relative to the book's expected correlation-breakdown scenario (a stress test, not just a historical average), not purely as a function of how comfortable net exposure currently looks.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the PM: 'net-neutral' doesn't mean 'free lunch on gross' — financing costs, margin requirements, and especially what happens to this book if the long/short correlation breaks down all scale with gross, independent of net. I'd set the gross limit based on a stress scenario where the hedge partially fails, not based on how comfortable things look under normal, well-behaved correlation.
commonMistakes: Treating gross exposure as a free variable as long as net exposure is managed
Not connecting gross exposure to financing cost and margin requirements directly
Setting gross limits from historical averages rather than a correlation-breakdown stress scenario
Assuming low net exposure implies low overall risk regardless of gross
keyPoints: Gross exposure drives financing costs (borrow costs, margin interest) independent of net exposure
Gross exposure drives margin requirements that can tighten suddenly under stress
High gross exposure amplifies losses specifically when long/short correlation unexpectedly breaks down
Gross limits should be stress-tested against a correlation-breakdown scenario, not set from calm-market averages

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Explains financing/margin costs scaling with gross exposure
Explains the correlation-breakdown amplification risk
Recommends a stress-based (not historical-average) approach to setting the limit

questions.title: What a Realistic Information Coefficient Looks Like
questions.prompt: A new researcher presents a signal with a measured Information Coefficient of 0.04 and is disappointed, expecting something closer to 0.5. How would you recalibrate their expectations, and what else about the IC besides its average value should they check?
questions.code: ic = signal.corrwith(fwd_return, axis=1).mean()
questions.modelAnswer: An IC of 0.04 is not disappointing in cross-sectional equity signal research — ICs in the 0.02 to 0.08 range are common for genuinely useful signals applied across a large universe and many periods, since this is a game of small, repeatable edges accumulated at scale, not big individual predictions. An IC near 0.5 would be extraordinarily, almost unbelievably strong for a real signal and should itself raise suspicion of a bug (likely lookahead bias) rather than celebration. Beyond the average IC value, the researcher should check its stability across periods: an IC that flips sign frequently or swings wildly from period to period is a much weaker signal than one with the same average IC that stays consistently positive, since an unstable IC suggests the average is being driven by a few lucky periods rather than a persistent, repeatable relationship.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell them to recalibrate immediately: 0.04 is a perfectly respectable number in this business, and an IC anywhere near 0.5 would make me suspicious of a bug before I'd get excited about it. The number I'd actually want to see next isn't a bigger average IC — it's the IC's stability over time. A consistent 0.03 beats an average of 0.06 that's secretly +0.3 one month and -0.2 the next.
commonMistakes: Expecting IC values comparable to a strong correlation in an unrelated, less noisy domain
Treating an unusually high IC as good news rather than a signal to check for a bug
Only looking at the average IC without checking its stability across periods
Not recognizing that this is a 'small, repeatable edges at scale' business, not big single predictions
keyPoints: Realistic cross-sectional equity ICs are commonly in the 0.02-0.08 range
An unusually high IC (e.g., near 0.5) should raise suspicion of a bug like lookahead bias
IC stability across periods matters as much as the average IC value
A consistent, modest IC is more trustworthy than a high but unstable one

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly recalibrates expectations about realistic IC magnitudes
Correctly flags an unusually high IC as suspicious rather than exciting
Recommends checking IC stability across periods

questions.title: Combining Two Highly Correlated Signals
questions.prompt: A researcher combines two signals at equal weight, both built from 12-month price momentum but using slightly different lookback windows, and finds the combination is 0.93 correlated with either signal alone. Why didn't this combination improve robustness, and what should be done instead?
questions.modelAnswer: Combining genuinely different, lowly-correlated signals can reduce idiosyncratic noise while keeping shared real signal — but these two signals aren't genuinely different; they're both measuring essentially the same underlying momentum effect with only a minor variation in lookback window, so their errors are highly correlated rather than independent. Adding them at equal weight doesn't give 'two votes' of independent information; it mostly doubles down on the same single underlying driver and gives it roughly double the influence it should have in a properly diversified blend, which is exactly why the combination ends up 0.93 correlated with either input alone — there was almost no diversification benefit to capture in the first place. The fix is to check the pairwise correlation matrix of candidate signals before combining: if two signals are this highly correlated, they should be treated as one signal (perhaps averaged together first, or simply picking one representative version) rather than as two independent votes in a combination.
questions.professionalAnswer: A 0.93 correlation between the combination and either single input is the tell that nothing was actually diversified here — these were never two signals, they were one signal wearing two slightly different costumes. I'd check the pairwise correlation matrix before combining anything going forward, and treat any pair above roughly 0.7-0.8 as a single signal for weighting purposes, not two.
commonMistakes: Assuming any two signals built differently are automatically diversifying
Not checking the pairwise correlation matrix before combining signals
Treating two highly correlated signal variants as independent votes in an equal-weight blend
Concluding the combination exercise failed rather than recognizing the inputs were never diversified
keyPoints: Combining benefits from genuinely different, lowly-correlated signals, not near-duplicate variants
Two highly correlated signals combined at equal weight mostly double down on one driver
Checking the pairwise correlation matrix before combining is a standard, necessary step
Highly correlated signal variants should be treated as one signal, not two independent inputs

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains why the combination provided no diversification benefit
Correctly connects this to the high correlation between the two inputs
Recommends checking correlation and treating correlated signals as one

questions.title: Why Naive Mean-Variance Optimization Often Underperforms Simpler Methods
questions.prompt: A backtest compares a naive mean-variance-optimized portfolio against a simple inverse-volatility-weighted portfolio using the same signal, and the 'optimal' mean-variance portfolio performs worse out-of-sample. Explain why this happens and isn't a contradiction.
questions.modelAnswer: Mean-variance optimization is only 'optimal' relative to its inputs — the expected return vector mu and the covariance matrix Sigma — and it's notoriously sensitive to small errors in mu specifically, since the optimizer (via inv(Sigma) @ mu) can amplify tiny estimation errors into wildly different, often extreme and concentrated weights. Because expected returns are genuinely hard to estimate precisely from noisy historical data, an optimizer built on noisy mu estimates ends up over-weighting whichever assets happened to look best by chance in the estimation sample, and that overfitting to noise is exactly what fails to generalize out-of-sample. Inverse-volatility weighting sidesteps this entirely by not requiring an expected-return estimate at all — it only needs volatility, which is estimated far more reliably than expected return — so it's far less prone to this specific overfitting failure mode, even though it's 'less optimal' on paper given perfect inputs. This isn't a contradiction: mean-variance is optimal in theory given perfect information, but inputs are never perfect in practice, and robustness to input error can matter more than theoretical optimality.
questions.professionalAnswer: This result shows up constantly in practice, and it's not actually surprising once you internalize how fragile mean-variance is to its mu input specifically. The optimizer is doing exactly what it's told — maximizing return for risk given the inputs — but if those inputs are mostly noise (which expected-return estimates usually are), it will confidently produce a very wrong-looking, concentrated answer. Inverse-volatility weighting just needs a much more reliably estimated input, which is why it tends to hold up better out-of-sample despite being 'less optimal' on paper.
commonMistakes: Treating the 'optimal' label as meaning it should always outperform simpler methods in practice
Not identifying expected-return estimation error specifically as the fragile input
Assuming the covariance matrix estimate is equally unreliable as the expected-return estimate
Concluding mean-variance optimization is theoretically wrong rather than practically fragile to noisy inputs
keyPoints: Mean-variance optimization is only optimal relative to its estimated inputs, mu and Sigma
The optimizer is especially sensitive to small errors in mu, which can produce extreme, concentrated weights
Inverse-volatility weighting avoids needing an expected-return estimate entirely
Theoretical optimality and practical robustness to input error are different things, and the latter can matter more

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains mean-variance's sensitivity to mu estimation error
Correctly explains why inverse-volatility weighting is more robust

questions.title: Estimating Capacity With the Square-Root Impact Model
questions.prompt: A strategy trades a stock with daily volatility of 2% and average daily volume (ADV) of $20 million. Using the square-root market impact model with a calibration constant c=1.0, estimate the impact cost (as a fraction of trade price) of an order equal to 25% of ADV, and discuss what this implies about the strategy's capacity.
questions.code: impact_cost ~= c * daily_vol * sqrt(order_size / ADV)
questions.modelAnswer: impact_cost = 1.0 * 0.02 * sqrt(0.25) = 0.02 * 0.5 = 0.01, or 1% of the trade's value. For an order equal to 25% of ADV on a $20 million ADV stock, that's a $5 million order incurring roughly 1% ($50,000) in estimated impact cost on that single trade. This implies real capacity constraints: if the strategy's gross edge per trade is, say, 0.5%, a 1% impact cost on a 25%-of-ADV order already exceeds the entire gross edge, meaning this strategy cannot profitably trade at this size in this name — capacity for this specific stock is well below $5 million per trade. Estimating capacity means finding the order size (and corresponding capital level) at which this same calculation brings impact cost up to roughly the gross edge, which sets the practical ceiling for how much capital the strategy can deploy before net performance degrades to unprofitable.
questions.professionalAnswer: I plug straight into the square-root formula and immediately compare the result to the strategy's actual gross edge — that comparison is the whole point. A 1% impact cost sounds small in isolation, but stacked against a modest gross edge it can wipe out the entire trade's profitability, which is exactly the kind of capacity ceiling a backtest run at a smaller, 'illustrative' size would never reveal.
questions.example: impact_cost = 1.0 * 0.02 * sqrt(0.25) = 0.01 (1%). On a $5M order (25% of $20M ADV), that's roughly $50,000 of impact cost.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to take the square root of the participation ratio rather than using it linearly
Not comparing the resulting impact cost against the strategy's actual gross edge
Assuming impact cost scales linearly with order size rather than with its square root
Treating this calibration-constant-dependent estimate as an exact, universal law rather than an approximation
keyPoints: impact_cost ~= c * daily_vol * sqrt(order_size / ADV)
Impact cost rises with the square root of participation, not linearly
Capacity is the size at which modeled impact cost erodes the gross edge to roughly zero

Correctly connects the result to a capacity implication

questions.title: A Backtest Inflated by Testing Thousands of Parameter Combinations
questions.prompt: A researcher swept roughly 3,000 combinations of a fast and slow moving-average crossover and reports the single best-performing combination's Sharpe ratio as the strategy's expected performance. What's wrong with this, and what would you ask to see before trusting the number?
questions.modelAnswer: This is a textbook data-snooping problem: if you test 3,000 parameter combinations against the same historical dataset, pure chance guarantees some of them will show an impressive-looking Sharpe ratio, not because they capture anything real, but because a finite history contains a limited amount of genuine signal and an enormous amount of noise, and with 3,000 tries you will find a combination that happened to fit that noise well. The reported 'best Sharpe' from this search is the maximum of thousands of noisy samples, a statistically different and far more optimistic quantity than a single honest test — it is not a trustworthy estimate of future performance. Before trusting the number, I'd ask to see the strategy's out-of-sample performance using parameters selected without looking at the holdout period, or better, a full walk-forward analysis that repeatedly re-fits on a rolling window and tests on the immediately following period — and I'd ask exactly how many combinations were tried, since that number directly tells you how skeptical to be of the in-sample result.
questions.professionalAnswer: The first question I'd ask is simply 'how many combinations did you try,' because that number alone tells me how much to discount the headline Sharpe before I look at anything else. A result selected as the best of 3,000 tries needs out-of-sample validation — ideally a proper walk-forward test — before it means anything; the in-sample number by itself is close to guaranteed to look good regardless of whether there's a real effect underneath it.
commonMistakes: Trusting the best in-sample Sharpe from a large parameter sweep as a performance estimate
Not asking how many combinations were tested before evaluating the result

questions.title: Designing a Walk-Forward Validation Scheme
questions.prompt: Design a walk-forward validation scheme for a strategy with 10 years of daily data, as an alternative to a single static train/test split. What does each 'roll' actually do, and why does this produce a more honest performance estimate?
questions.modelAnswer: A walk-forward scheme repeatedly re-fits the strategy's parameters on a rolling window of past data and tests on the immediately following period, then rolls forward in time and repeats — for example, fit on years 1-3, test on year 4; fit on years 2-4, test on year 5; and so on through the full 10 years. Each 'roll' simulates exactly what a real researcher would have had to do in practice: periodically re-optimize parameters using only the data that would actually have been available up to that point, never peeking into the future test period during fitting. This produces a more honest estimate than a single static train/test split because it generates many independent out-of-sample test periods rather than just one, giving a fuller picture of how consistently the strategy would have performed if parameters were genuinely re-estimated through time rather than fixed once using the full history — a single static split only tells you about one particular out-of-sample stretch, while walk-forward averages over many.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd set it up so every single test period is strictly information the fitting step never saw — fit on a trailing window, test on the next chunk, then slide the whole window forward and repeat. The honesty comes from doing this many times instead of once: a single train/test split gives you one out-of-sample data point, which could just be a lucky or unlucky stretch, while walk-forward gives you a whole distribution of out-of-sample results built the way a real researcher would actually have operated.
commonMistakes: Fitting parameters once on the full history and only testing walk-forward-style, which isn't actually walk-forward
Allowing any look-ahead across the roll boundary between fit and test windows
Treating walk-forward as equivalent to, rather than more rigorous than, a single static split
Not explaining why multiple rolls give a fuller picture than one split
keyPoints: Each roll re-fits parameters on a trailing window and tests on the immediately following period
The window then advances forward in time and the process repeats
This simulates how a real researcher would have had to re-optimize using only information available at each point
Walk-forward produces many out-of-sample test periods instead of just one, giving a fuller, more honest picture

questions.title: A Backtest Filling at an Impossible Price
questions.prompt: A backtest generates a signal from bar N's closing price and fills the resulting trade at bar N+1's closing price. What's wrong with this fill assumption, and what's the standard, defensible fix for daily-bar data?
questions.modelAnswer: Filling at bar N+1's close, having generated the signal from bar N's close, smuggles in a full extra day of favorable-or-unfavorable price movement with no justification — it quietly assumes the ability to trade at a price that won't actually be observed until the end of that next bar, which is just as physically impossible as trading on bar N's own close in the first place. A market order placed as soon as the signal is known (right after bar N's close) can only fill at the next price actually quoted to the market, which for daily bar data is conventionally bar N+1's open — the most common, defensible default fill assumption without more granular intraday data. The fill price should also layer in realistic slippage and market impact on top of that reference price, rather than assuming a perfectly clean fill at the exact open print.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd flag this immediately: using N+1's close for both the fill and an entire day's worth of price action between the signal and the trade is a second lookahead problem hiding right next to the obvious one. The fix is mechanical — fill at N+1's open, the earliest price actually achievable once the signal is known — and then stack slippage and impact on top of that, rather than assuming a magically clean fill at a price you couldn't have known about until the bar closed.
commonMistakes: Not recognizing that filling at N+1 close still contains a hidden lookahead problem
Assuming the fix is to fill at N's own close instead of N+1's open
Forgetting to layer slippage and market impact on top of the corrected reference price
Treating this as a minor detail rather than a real backtest realism issue
keyPoints: Filling at bar N+1's close after a signal from bar N's close smuggles in an extra day of unearned price movement
The standard, defensible fill assumption for daily-bar market orders is bar N+1's open
Slippage and market impact should be layered on top of this reference price, not ignored
Every fill assumption should be checked for whether it could have actually happened in real time

Correctly states the standard fix (N+1's open)

questions.title: Computing Calmar and Omega Ratios
questions.prompt: A strategy has an annualized return of 14%, a maximum drawdown of -10%, and its daily returns show $1.15 of weighted gains above zero for every $1.00 of weighted losses below zero. Compute the Calmar ratio and the Omega ratio (threshold = 0), and explain what each one tells you that the other doesn't.
questions.code:
Calmar = annualized_return / abs(max_drawdown)
Omega(L) = gains_above_L / losses_below_L
questions.modelAnswer: Calmar = 0.14 / abs(-0.10) = 0.14/0.10 = 1.4. Omega(0) = 1.15/1.00 = 1.15. Calmar tells you how much annualized return the strategy earned relative to its single worst peak-to-trough decline — a Calmar of 1.4 means the strategy earned about 1.4x its worst drawdown, annualized, which is the number an allocator focused on 'how bad could my worst stretch be' cares about most. Omega instead uses the entire return distribution rather than two summary numbers (mean and variance, or return and max drawdown): an Omega of 1.15 means the dollar-weighted upside above the threshold outweighs the dollar-weighted downside below it by 15%, capturing distributional shape (skew, fat tails) that neither Calmar nor Sharpe/Sortino directly sees. The two measures can disagree because they're built from entirely different parts of the return series — Calmar from one worst-case event, Omega from the full shape of gains versus losses — so a strategy can look strong on one and merely adequate on the other.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd compute both and present them side by side rather than picking a favorite — Calmar answers the worst-case-pain question, Omega answers the whole-distribution-shape question, and neither substitutes for the other. A Calmar of 1.4 and an Omega of 1.15 paint a decent but not spectacular picture either way here, and I'd want to know in advance which question the reader actually cares about before leading with one ratio over the other.
commonMistakes: Confusing Calmar's drawdown-based measure with Omega's full-distribution measure
Forgetting to take the absolute value of max drawdown before dividing
Assuming the two ratios should generally agree with each other
Not explaining what Omega captures that mean/variance-based measures like Sharpe miss

Omega(L) = weighted gains above threshold L / weighted losses below L
Calmar isolates worst-case pain; Omega captures the full return distribution's shape
The two measures can disagree because they're built from different aspects of the return series

Correctly computes the Omega ratio
Correctly explains what each one captures that the other doesn't

questions.title: Information Ratio vs Sharpe Ratio
questions.prompt: A long-only equity strategy has a perfectly respectable Sharpe ratio of 0.9, but its Information Ratio versus its benchmark is only 0.15. How can both be true at once, and which number should a benchmark-relative allocator actually care about more?
questions.code:
IR = mean(active_return) / std(active_return)
active_return = strategy_return - benchmark_return
questions.modelAnswer: Both numbers can be true simultaneously because they measure fundamentally different things: Sharpe measures the strategy's own absolute return relative to its own total volatility, in isolation, while the Information Ratio measures the strategy's return relative to a specific benchmark, divided by tracking error (the volatility of the difference between strategy and benchmark returns). A long-only strategy can have a solid absolute Sharpe largely because it's riding the market's own return (which the benchmark also captures), while adding very little in excess of what simply holding the benchmark would have delivered — producing a high Sharpe but a low IR. For a benchmark-relative allocator — someone evaluating the strategy specifically against 'could I have just held the benchmark instead' — the Information Ratio is the more relevant number, since it directly answers whether the manager added meaningful, consistent value beyond what the benchmark alone provides; the Sharpe ratio alone would make the strategy look better than it actually performed relative to that specific, relevant alternative.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the allocator: Sharpe can look great mostly because the market itself did well, which the benchmark also captured — that's not manager skill, that's beta. The Information Ratio is the number that actually isolates whether this manager earned their fee by beating the benchmark consistently, and a 0.15 there is a pretty unremarkable result, Sharpe of 0.9 notwithstanding.
commonMistakes: Assuming Sharpe and Information Ratio should generally track each other closely
Not recognizing that a long-only strategy's Sharpe is heavily influenced by overall market direction
Confusing tracking error with the strategy's own total volatility
Not identifying the Information Ratio as the more relevant number for a benchmark-relative evaluation
keyPoints: Sharpe measures absolute return relative to the strategy's own total volatility
Information Ratio measures return relative to a benchmark, divided by tracking error
A long-only strategy can show a solid Sharpe mostly from riding market beta while adding little versus its benchmark
A benchmark-relative allocator should weight the Information Ratio more heavily than Sharpe alone

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains how both numbers can be true simultaneously
Correctly defines the Information Ratio and tracking error
Correctly identifies IR as more relevant for a benchmark-relative evaluation

questions.title: Computing a Sharpe Ratio's Standard Error With Lo's Formula
questions.prompt: A strategy's daily Sharpe ratio is 0.045, measured over n=500 trading days. Using Lo's approximation, compute the standard error of the annualized Sharpe ratio and its 95% confidence interval.
questions.code:
SE(Sharpe_daily) ~= sqrt((1 + 0.5*Sharpe_daily^2) / n)
Sharpe_ann = Sharpe_daily * sqrt(252)
SE_ann = SE_daily * sqrt(252)
questions.modelAnswer: SE(Sharpe_daily) = sqrt((1 + 0.5*0.045^2) / 500) = sqrt((1 + 0.0010125)/500) = sqrt(1.0010125/500) ≈ sqrt(0.0020020) ≈ 0.04475. Annualized Sharpe = 0.045 * sqrt(252) ≈ 0.045*15.87 ≈ 0.714. Annualized SE = 0.04475 * sqrt(252) ≈ 0.04475*15.87 ≈ 0.710. 95% CI = 0.714 ± 1.96*0.710 ≈ 0.714 ± 1.391, giving roughly [-0.68, 2.10]. The point estimate of 0.714 looks like a respectable Sharpe, but the confidence interval is wide enough to include clearly negative values, meaning this particular sample cannot rule out that the true underlying Sharpe ratio is actually negative.
questions.professionalAnswer: I compute the daily standard error first using Lo's formula, then scale both the Sharpe and its standard error by sqrt(252) consistently — scaling only one of them is a common mistake. The confidence interval here stretching from clearly negative to over 2 is exactly the kind of sobering result this formula is meant to surface: a seemingly solid 0.71 Sharpe from 500 days of data just isn't backed by enough sample size to rule out a true Sharpe of zero or below.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the 0.5*Sharpe^2 term inside Lo's formula
Annualizing the Sharpe ratio but forgetting to annualize its standard error by the same sqrt(252) factor
Using 1.96 incorrectly or forgetting it entirely when building the 95% interval
Treating the wide confidence interval as invalidating the point estimate rather than contextualizing it
keyPoints: Lo's formula: SE(Sharpe) ~= sqrt((1 + 0.5*Sharpe^2) / n), computed at the same frequency as the Sharpe ratio
Both the Sharpe ratio and its standard error scale by the same sqrt(annualization factor)
A 95% CI uses point estimate +/- 1.96 * standard error
A seemingly solid point-estimate Sharpe can still have a confidence interval including zero or negative values

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly computes the daily standard error via Lo's formula
Correctly annualizes both the Sharpe ratio and its standard error
Correctly computes and interprets the 95% confidence interval

questions.title: Interpreting a Bootstrap Confidence Interval That Straddles Zero
questions.prompt: A bootstrap resampling of a strategy's daily returns produces a 95% confidence interval for its annualized Sharpe ratio of [-0.35, 2.45], with 93% of the resampled Sharpe ratios coming out positive. How would you explain this result to a PM who sees the positive point estimate and wants to proceed, and what would you actually recommend?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd explain that the bootstrap is directly telling us how much uncertainty surrounds the point estimate: based on resampling this exact historical return series thousands of times, there's roughly a 93% chance the true underlying Sharpe ratio is positive — which sounds reassuring on its face, but also means there's roughly a 1-in-14 chance it isn't, for a strategy whose point-estimate Sharpe looks like a clear 'solid' result under the usual rule of thumb. This doesn't mean the strategy is bad; it means the sample isn't long enough yet to be highly confident the apparent edge is real rather than a reasonably likely but not certain draw of noise. I'd recommend against proceeding at full size based on this evidence alone — either gathering more data/running longer before committing significant capital, sizing any initial allocation conservatively given the real uncertainty, or seeking additional corroborating evidence (an economic rationale for the edge, out-of-sample validation) rather than treating the positive point estimate as sufficient on its own.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd lead with the number that actually matters here, not the Sharpe point estimate: a roughly 1-in-14 chance the true edge isn't even positive. That's not a disaster, but it's not a green light either — I'd push back on sizing this at full conviction yet, and suggest either more data, a smaller initial allocation, or some independent corroborating evidence before treating this as a confirmed edge.

Failing to propose a concrete next step (more data, smaller sizing, corroborating evidence)

questions.title: Writing an Abstract That Leads With the Net Number
questions.prompt: A strategy's gross Sharpe is 0.76, but net of realistic transaction costs it's 0.42. A first draft of the performance report's abstract leads with the gross Sharpe. How would you rewrite the abstract's opening, and why does the order matter?
questions.modelAnswer: The most common mistake in a strategy write-up is leading with the gross number because it's the bigger, more flattering one. I'd rewrite the abstract to state the net Sharpe (0.42) before a reader has a chance to anchor on the gross figure — something like: 'Net of realistic transaction costs, the strategy's Sharpe is 0.42; gross of costs it is 0.76.' The order matters because readers anchor heavily on whichever number they see first, and a report that leads with gross risks leaving a misleadingly optimistic first impression even if the net number appears later in the document — by the time a skeptical reader reaches it, the gross number has often already shaped their expectations. Leading with net also signals that the report is being honest about costs upfront rather than making the reader dig for the real number.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd flip the sentence order without changing a single fact in it — net first, gross second, exactly the opposite of the draft. It's a small edit with an outsized effect: whichever number a reader sees first is the one that sets their expectations, and I'd rather the report set honest expectations from its very first sentence than have a reader anchor on a number that isn't what they'd actually experience.

Treating this as a stylistic preference rather than a substantive honesty issue

questions.title: Writing a Limitations Section a Reader Will Actually Trust
questions.prompt: A performance report's limitations section currently reads 'no major limitations were identified.' Why does that sentence actually hurt the report's credibility, and what should a genuine limitations section for a strategy backtested over 2010-2024 realistically include?
questions.modelAnswer: A limitations section that lists nothing is a limitations section nobody trusts — every real strategy backtest has genuine limitations, and claiming otherwise signals either that the author didn't look hard enough or isn't being fully honest, both of which undermine confidence in the rest of the report. A genuine limitations section for a 2010-2024 backtest should name plainly: the sample period includes relatively few truly severe crisis events (tail behavior is estimated from thin evidence), any changes in the universe or data composition over that span, the strategy's capacity ceiling and at what capital level costs would erode the net edge, and whether the strategy's typical risk profile (e.g., near-zero beta) has ever meaningfully deviated during stress, with a specific example if one exists. None of these invalidate the research — naming them explicitly is exactly what makes the research credible to a skeptical reader.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the author directly: 'no limitations' reads as either lazy or dishonest to any experienced reviewer, and it will cost more credibility than any specific limitation ever would. A real limitations section names the thin tail-event sample, any universe changes over the period, the capacity ceiling, and any known instance where the strategy's risk profile broke from its usual pattern — specific, concrete items, not a blanket reassurance.

Treating limitations as weaknesses to minimize rather than information that builds credibility

questions.title: A Rapid P&L Mental-Math Drill
questions.prompt: In a trading interview, you're asked: 'You're long 800 shares at $42.50. The stock rises to $44.75. What's your P&L, and if instead you were short 800 shares at that same entry, what would it be?' Walk through both answers quickly and explain the sign logic.
questions.code:
Long P&L = (exit - entry) * shares
Short P&L = (entry - exit) * shares
questions.modelAnswer: Long position: (44.75 - 42.50) * 800 = 2.25 * 800 = $1,800 profit — a long position gains when the price rises, so exit minus entry, times shares, is the correct direction. Short position with the same entry and exit: (42.50 - 44.75) * 800 = -2.25 * 800 = -$1,800, a $1,800 loss — a short position gains when the price falls, so the formula flips to entry minus exit; here the price rose, so the short loses exactly what the long gained. The sign logic is symmetric: long P&L and short P&L on the same price move are always equal and opposite, since one side's gain is exactly the other side's loss on the identical move.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd answer both in one breath using the symmetry: whatever the long made, the short lost, dollar for dollar, on the same move. I practice this pattern specifically so the sign never trips me up under time pressure — long is exit minus entry, short is entry minus exit, and the two numbers should always be exact mirror images of each other.
commonMistakes: Getting the sign backwards on the short position's formula
Not recognizing that long and short P&L on the identical move must be exact mirror images
Taking too long to compute a simple arithmetic drill under interview time pressure
Forgetting to multiply by share count after computing the per-share price difference
keyPoints: Long P&L = (exit price - entry price) * shares
Short P&L = (entry price - exit price) * shares
Long and short P&L on the identical price move are always equal and opposite

questions.title: Evaluating a Profit-Share Offer vs a Steady Bank-Desk Offer
questions.prompt: You have two competing offers at the same seniority level: a prop trading firm with a lower base salary but a profit-share structure heavily tied to your own individual PnL, and a bank quant desk with a higher, steadier base and a bonus tied more to overall division performance. How do you actually compare these beyond just the headline base salary numbers?
questions.modelAnswer: Comparing just the base salaries misses the point, since the two structures carry fundamentally different variance: the prop firm's profit-share model can pay far more in a strong individual year and far less in a weak one, while the bank desk's structure is steadier and tied more to overall division results rather than directly to your own trades. I'd evaluate the whole package — bonus determination method (individual PnL vs. team vs. discretionary), vesting schedule on any deferred compensation, and realistic timeline to meaningful bonus eligibility — and weigh these alongside non-compensation factors that matter just as much: strategy and risk-culture fit, whether the environment rewards honest research or overselling results, the mentorship and learning curve available, and what the role actually does day to day (research-heavy, trading-heavy, or infrastructure-heavy roles can carry the same title at different firms). questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't compare these on base salary alone — that's comparing two different bets, not two similar offers. I'd map out the full range of outcomes each structure could realistically produce, be honest with myself about how much compensation variance I can actually tolerate, and then weigh that against the things that tend to matter more day to day than the number on the offer letter: who's going to teach me something, and does this firm's culture actually reward the kind of rigorous, honest research I want to be doing.

questions.title: The Single-Index Model's Connection to CAPM
questions.prompt: Explain how the single-index model, written as a regression, is literally how beta is estimated in practice, and why this regression form is also the simplest possible factor model.
questions.code: Ri = alpha_i + beta_i * Rm + epsilon_i
questions.modelAnswer: The single-index model, Ri = alpha_i + beta_i*Rm + epsilon_i, is estimated via ordinary least squares, regressing an asset's historical returns against the market's historical returns — this is literally how beta is computed in practice: beta_i is simply the OLS regression slope, and alpha_i is the intercept, capturing whatever average return isn't explained by market exposure. This is also exactly CAPM's own structure, just presented as a regression rather than an expected-value equation: CAPM's beta_i*(E[Rm]-Rf) term and the single-index model's beta_i*Rm term are the same quantity, estimated the same way. It's the simplest possible factor model because it uses exactly one systematic factor (the market); Fama-French's three-factor model is the identical regression framework extended to three factors (market, SMB, HML) instead of one, and any further multi-factor model is just the same structure with more terms added to the right-hand side.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd point out that this isn't a separate concept from CAPM at all — it's CAPM's own math, just written as a regression you'd actually run on real data. Beta isn't some separately-derived theoretical quantity; it's literally the slope you get back from regressing an asset's returns on the market's returns. Once you see that, Fama-French and every other multi-factor model are obviously the exact same regression idea, just with more explanatory variables added to the right-hand side.

Not recognizing CAPM's expected-return equation and the single-index regression as the same underlying structure

questions.title: Presenting Residual Gamma and Vega to an Interviewer
questions.prompt: An interviewer reviewing your options-hedging capstone project asks: 'You flattened delta — so is the portfolio hedged?' How do you answer in a way that demonstrates real understanding rather than overstating what you accomplished?
questions.modelAnswer: I'd answer directly: no, not fully — flattening delta neutralizes the portfolio's first-order sensitivity to a small move in the underlying, which is the specific thing a delta-hedge is designed to do, but the portfolio still carries nonzero gamma and vega. Nonzero gamma means the hedge itself will drift out of balance as soon as the underlying actually moves, since the options' deltas shift while the stock hedge's delta stays fixed at 1 — so this hedge needs to be rebalanced, not left in place. Nonzero vega means the portfolio still has a real view on implied volatility that the stock-based hedge does nothing to address, since a share of stock has zero vega. I'd frame the answer as: the hedge did exactly what it promised, no more and no less, and being precise about what it doesn't cover is as important as describing what it does.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd never answer 'yes, fully hedged' to that question — I'd say the delta-hedge did its specific job, and then immediately name what's still exposed: gamma, which means this hedge has a shelf life and needs rebalancing, and vega, which means there's still a real volatility bet sitting in the book that the stock trade does nothing about. Interviewers ask this exact question because they want to see whether a candidate overstates a result or can precisely state its limits, and I'd rather demonstrate the latter.
commonMistakes: Answering 'yes, fully hedged' without qualification
Not naming gamma and vega specifically as the remaining exposures
Failing to explain why gamma means the hedge needs rebalancing rather than being a one-time fix
Missing the opportunity to demonstrate precision about the result's actual scope
keyPoints: A delta-hedge only addresses first-order sensitivity to the underlying's price
Nonzero gamma means the hedge will drift out of balance and needs rebalancing
Nonzero vega means a real volatility exposure remains that the stock hedge can't address
